== Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (はしらまつさいとうしんじ) is the principal ritual of Kosuge Shrine (小菅神社), which was formerly held annually on July 15. Currently, it is conducted once every three years on a Sunday in mid-July. It is also known as Matsuko. It is designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}} (designated as "Kosuge's Hashiramatsu Ritual"). In the plaza in front of the Kosuge Shrine Satomiya Lecture Hall (里宮講堂), two pillar pines, each 4 meters tall and bound together with assorted wood tied with straw, are erected. A figure known as Matsukamiko (松神子) ascends these two pillars, and the speed with which it ignites them using flint and steel is contested. It is said that if the eastern pillar triumphs, it portends universal peace, whereas if the western pillar wins, it is an omen for a bountiful harvest. This test, originally performed by Shugendō practitioners in conjunction with prayers for abundant crops, is said to have been passed down to the present. Along with {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}} and {{ill|Iinawa Mountain|ja|飯縄山|lt=Iitsuna|lt_ja=飯綱}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Ozunu|ja|役小角}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治時代}} due to the {{ill|Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|ja|神仏分離}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre‑modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. However, according to several ancient documents that recount the shrine’s history, the Shugendō temple Ganryūji (元隆寺), founded by En no Ozunu, is considered the origin of Kosugeyama. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Horse-Headed Kannon|ja|馬頭観音}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. En no Ozunu subsequently enshrined Kosuge Gongen as the principal deity and, in addition, invited and enshrined seven deities—{{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|lt=Kumano|lt_ja=熊野}}, {{ill|Kanminesanjin|ja|金峯山寺|lt=Kanminesanjin|lt_ja=金峯山}} ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野}}), {{ill|Hakusan|ja|白山}}, {{ill|Tateyama|ja|立山}}, Sannō, Hayayuki, and {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}}—as shown in Table 1. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文}} ({{ill|1542|ja|1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō Era|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|lt_ja=大同}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|lt=Sengoku period|lt_ja=戦国時代}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji Era|ja|弘治 (日本)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=弘治}} ({{ill|1557|ja|1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku}} ({{ill|1567|ja|1567}}) and the {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō Era|ja|慶長}} (around {{ill|1600|ja|1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5年〈1600年〉/{{ill|Genroku Era|ja|元禄|lt=Genroku|lt_ja=元年}} 〈{{ill|1688|ja|1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:小菅神社]] == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. Table 2 shows the major historical sources related to Kosugeyama. understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:歴史]] === 先史時代 === 他の修験霊場にも見られるように、小菅山にもまた自然信仰の層を見出すことができ、そうした基層をまず見ておくべきであろう。小菅山のある飯山市小菅集落の周辺では、[[縄文時代]]にさかのぼる集落遺跡が発見されており、[[弥生時代]]中期には稲作が開始されていたことが判明している。すなわち、早い時期から小菅山の一帯には定住が見られたのである。すぐ北に[[越後国]]をひかえた、世界でも有数の豪雪地帯でありながら、そうした定住が可能であったのは、雪と森、そしてそれらがもたらす豊かな水のゆえであった。そして修験入山以前の時代には、そうした自然の実り豊かさに対する信仰（水分神信仰）が行われていたことが分かっている。 === 小菅山の確立 === こうした自然信仰的な基層に対し、小菅山の信仰に社寺としての形態が与えられた年代、すなわち小菅山の歴史的創建は、おそくとも[[平安時代]]後期までのことと考えられている。小菅山にまつわる諸史資料のなかで、社伝の木造馬頭観世音菩薩坐像が平安時代後期の作と推定されるためである。 平安時代後期はまた、[[本地垂迹]]思想の定着と、中世熊野御幸の隆盛期でもある。小菅山を含めた北信州一帯においても、[[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|後白河院]]撰の『[[梁塵秘抄]]』に戸隠山がうたわれていることから推測されるように、熊野修験が入り込んできただけでなく、小菅山の確立に寄与したものと考えられている。事実、小菅山を含む小菅荘一帯には、八所権現だけでなく、熊野社も数多く勧請されており、小菅山の霊場としての確立期に熊野修験の活動があったことを知ることができる。 なお、この時期までに小菅山が確立していたことを伝える史料に、社伝の菩提院曼荼羅がある。菩提院曼荼羅は、中国から輸入された絹地に畿内で彩色されたものであり、制作年代は鎌倉時代末期から[[南北朝時代 (日本)|南北朝時代]]にかけてと推定されている。このような希少品を蔵することからも、小菅山が一定の勢力をともなって確立したことをうかがい知ることができるだろう。 === 南北朝時代から隆盛期まで === [[鎌倉幕府]]崩壊から南北朝時代の始まりころまでには、小菅山を含む[[小菅荘]]一帯は、南に[[高梨氏]]勢力下の[[犬飼荘]]、北に[[市河氏]]の[[志久見郷湯山荘]]に接し、両者の緩衝地帯として戦略的な要地となっていた。しかし、南北朝の騒乱はついにこの地に及び、[[延文]]元年（[[1356]]、南朝[[Shōhei]]11年）には、志久見郷侵攻を企てた南朝党の高梨氏が逆撃を受けて小菅にて惨敗している。その後、高梨氏は勢力を盛り返し、市河氏に対する復仇戦に勝利を収めているが、この頃を境に南朝党の勢力は衰微し、両朝統一の趨勢に従った。以後、Ashikaga Shogunateの支配が安定すると共に、小菅山は修験霊場としての隆盛期を迎えることになる。 [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|加耶吉利堂跡]] この頃の小菅山の隆盛を示すものとして、この時期に行われた元隆寺での造営を伝える文書がある。[[応永]]13年（[[1422]]）には、加耶吉利堂が建立され、堂内には近隣の土豪らによって著色観音三十三身板絵（応永年間在銘）が寄進された。[[永享]]2年（[[1430]]）からは4年の歳月をかけて、元隆寺の宮社坊中寺観が再建された。[[永正]]5年（[[1508]]）9月には、奥社内の宮殿が建立され、天文15年（[[1546]]）には、桐竹鳳凰文透彫奥社脇立二面が製作されている。これらの記録からすると、16世紀の半ばまで、小菅山では造営が営々と続けられており、それを可能にするだけの繁栄があったのである。 なお、応永12年（[[1421]]）には、将軍[[足利義持]]が大納言法印忠意に[[禅林寺 (京都市)|禅林寺]]永観堂若王子別当職などとともに、社領として信濃国小菅荘ほかを安堵したとの記録が残されている『信濃史料』第7巻。。この件に関する資料の大半を蔵する禅林寺若王子社は、もともと[[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|後白河院]]が[[永暦]]年間に熊野三山の土を運んで熊野権現を勧請したと伝えられる社である。若王子社領として領知されたことを述べるこの文書から、この時期までに小菅山が京都の支配下におかれていたことが確認できる。[[応仁]]元年（[[1467]]）にも将軍[[足利義政]]から大納言法印忠雅に同様の領知があった『信濃史料』第8巻。。 === 戦国時代 === 戦国時代における信濃は[[上杉氏]]と[[武田氏]]の争覇の舞台であり、その騒乱から小菅山も逃れることはできなかった。実際、既述の謙信願文は、上杉謙信が[[Takeda Shingen|武田晴信]]に合戦を挑むに際してのものである。上杉氏と武田氏の一連の戦いで、小菅山を含む[[小菅集落 (飯山市)|小菅荘]]一帯も戦禍に巻き込まれたことは間違いなく、武田氏領に帰した時期があったのも事実である。とはいえ、略縁起が伝えるように武田氏の侵攻によって一挙に荒廃したとするのは過度な誇張である。武田領となった後、[[天正]]7年（[[1579]]）2月25日付で、武田勝頼は「小菅」と越後赤沢の間の連絡の便を図るため、人家を置かせており、小菅の地の戦略的・交通的な重要性は依然として認知されていたからである。 この時期はまた、京都からの自立の時期でもあったようである。永禄11年（[[1567]]）の禅林寺若王子神社領覚書『信濃史料』第13巻。によれば、小菅荘からの年貢が不達である旨が述べられており、この頃までには京都の支配から脱していたことが推定される。 [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|護摩堂（大聖院跡）]] === 近世以降の小菅 === その後、天正10年（[[1582]]）3月に織田・徳川連合軍の武田領侵攻により武田氏が滅亡し、川中島四郡は[[織田氏]]の家臣・[[森長可]]が支配する。同年6月の[[本能寺の変]]により「[[天正壬午の乱]]」が発生すると、小菅は越後国の[[上杉景勝]]領となり、情勢が安定を見るとともに奥社本殿が再建された。 再建にあたっては、小菅山の経営にあたっていた別当寺院大聖院のほか、18坊が願主となり、天正19年（[[1591]]）に完成している。完成の2年後、[[文禄]]2年（[[1593]]）には、[[越後国|越後]]の人、金丸与八郎が鉄製鰐口を奉納している「小菅神社所蔵棟札銘写」および「小菅神社所蔵鉄製鰐口」、いずれも『信濃史料』第17巻所収。。この様に、度重なる混乱に巻き込まれながらも、越後からの鰐口奉納があったことに見られるように、小菅の宗教的権威は依然として衰えなかった。 慶長3年（[[1598]]）2月、上杉氏の会津移封にともなって大聖院が移転した。このことにより、小菅山の再建が頓挫したとされるが、それは必ずしも正しくない。慶長11年（[[1606]]）には、皆川氏より絵馬2面が寄進されており、大聖院の移転と小菅山の聖地としての性格は別個のものであった。また、新たな別当に神袋坊を迎えて大聖院自体も存続しているのである。

大聖院の移転が小菅の退勢をもたらさなかったことを裏付けるものとして、大聖院と小菅村の石高記録がある（表3）。文禄4年（[[1594]]）に実施された上杉領内検地の記録『文禄三年上納員数録』によれば、大聖院の知行高は58石とされ、小菅の集落全体を下回る。以後、近世の記録を見ても、小菅の石高と大聖院の知行高には開きがあることが分かる。しばしば大聖院と小菅は同一視され、大聖院が小菅に及ぼした影響力ないし支配力は非常に大きなものと見なされる。しかし、上記のような石高記録が示すところによれば、実際には大聖院は小菅の一部であったのである。 大聖院が小菅の一部であったという論点はさらに、小菅神社の主要な神事である[[#柱松柴灯神事|柱松柴灯神事]]の形態によっても補強されるだろう。 [[image:P8220504_Satosha_hall.JPG|thumb|right|250px|里宮講堂。講堂の前庭で柱松柴灯神事が行われる。]] 柱松柴灯神事は修験道の祭事とされ、元隆寺が大きな役割を担ったとされてきた。しかし、略縁起やそれに由来する通説的理解の説くところによれば、元隆寺は戦国期の荒廃以後、再建されることもなく荒廃するにまかされて、[[江戸時代|近世]]にさしかかる[[17世紀]]初めには、すでに廃墟と化していたのではなかったのだろうか。戦国期に元隆寺が衰退したままであったのならば、なぜ柱松柴灯神事のような大きな祭事を執行・維持できたのかが説明できない。また、寺院が主導したというならば、[[明治]]期の廃仏毀釈にもかかわらず、祭が廃絶しなかったのかを説明できない。さらに、諸史料に見られる柱松柴灯神事の記述を追ってみると、「修験神輿前において柱松柴灯護摩を修す」（来由記）、（奥院にて）「馬頭の護摩を修す」「天下太平のために奥院におゐて長日の護摩を始終す」（略縁起）などとあり、修験寺院の祭事としての性格が明瞭である。それにもかかわらず、今日の柱松柴灯神事には護摩にかかわる儀礼は存在しておらず、寺院による関与も見られないのである。今日の神事に用いられる山伏面・山姥面が江戸時代初期に製作されていることや、奥社参道の杉並木や小菅に残されている宗教建築の多くが江戸時代に整備されたものであることが判明しており、その様に積極的な霊場経営が行われていたという事実は、通説的理解と整合しない。以上のように、通説的理解はいくつもの矛盾を含んでいるのである。 そうした通説的理解とは異なる小菅の近世の姿を描き出している点で、注目すべき民俗史料がある。[[天明]]3年（[[1783]]）に取り決められた「御祭禮日市中村定連判帳」である。この文書は、祭礼日の治安維持や、参詣者を目当てにした市の管理、市に出店する店からの金銭徴収などが定められており、要約するならば里人による祭礼運営の規約である。この文書が示すところからすると、祭礼に出店する商人たちからの金銭徴収は村の収入となっていた。そのため、市を栄させるために必要な配慮がなされており、そのあらわれがこの文書である。このことが示すところは、祭礼が小菅の村の世俗的運営に委ねられていたということに他ならない。 以上からすると、中世から近世への移行期にあって、霊場としての小菅の統治は、領主の庇護下にある寺院の手から里人の手に移り、それとともに祭礼の性格も宗教的なものから、観客（参詣者）に見せることに重きを置いた愉楽的・観光的な性格に移行して行ったと考えられる。そして、そのために、明治の廃仏毀釈を経ても柱松神事は途絶えることがなかったのである。 小菅山の歴史についての通説的理解は、元隆寺やその別当寺院たる大聖院の役割を非常に大きなものとして描いてきた。しかしながら、そうした通説的理解が正しくないことが、以上から浮かび上がってくる。戦国期の兵乱を経てもなお、元隆寺の勢威は衰えたわけではなかった。しかしながら、近世以降の小菅山においては、里人の世俗的な霊場経営が優越し、元隆寺が霊場経営に果たした役割は逆に縮小して行ったのである。 === 近代 === 明治時代になって、神仏分離令が発されると、小菅山においても小菅神社と大聖院が分離されることとなった。しかし、[[明治]]2年（[[1868]]）には大聖院別当職にあった武内英真が神職に就き、仏式什器を菩提寺に移管する一方で、小菅山八所大権現を小菅社八所と改め、今日の小菅神社の直接的な起源に当たる神社が成立した。 明治3年（[[1871]]）に[[社格#近代社格制度| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|type]]制度がしかれると、小菅神社は、[[1873]]（明治6年）に郷社に列せられ、[[1933]]（昭和8年）には県社に列せられている。[[1909]]（明治42年）には、小菅村内の村社19社と無格社5社を合祀し、[[1946]]（[[昭和]]21年）の分社寺まで、一村の村民全てを氏子とした。[[1951]]（昭和29年）の神道指令までは、例祭日には県の奉幣使の参向があった。 == 小菅神社神域内の文化財 == 小菅山は、自然信仰の時代には水分神が祀られ、後に熊野修験の手によって霊場として確立された。そのため、[[熊野神社|熊野社]]が各所に見られる。来由記などに記されたところによれば、神社結界地となっていたのは、大倉崎口（現在の飯山市大字常盤）、関沢口、前坂口、神戸口の4箇所で、それぞれ鳥居が設けられており、神域への入口となっていた。この結界内部には、小菅神社に由縁ある社寺・史跡・民俗が今日に伝えられている。 ; 奥社本殿（重要文化財） : 小菅神社の本殿。大聖院跡地護摩堂から続く参道をぬけ、溶岩性の岩石が露出する急峻な登山道を進んだ、標高820m付近にある。天正19年（1592年）の修復記録があり、棟札によれば小野源之丞政高なる大工が修造にあたったとある。小菅神社の祭神8柱を祀る。 : 屋根は入母屋造、妻入、銅板葺き。桁行・梁間とも4間（「間」は柱間の数を指す）。柱間を正側面とも偶数とする（中央に柱が来る）のは、社寺建築には珍しい。組物は出三斗（でみつと）、軒は二軒繁垂木（ふたのきしげだるき）とする。東・南・西の3面に切目縁をめぐらし、東面は後方3間分に下屋（げや）を設ける。北面は岩窟が迫っている。南面は斜面に張り出した[[懸造]]とし、西側に階段をつけて西の縁から社殿に上るようになっている。建物は天文年間（1532 - 1554年）の建立とみられ、内部に安置される禅宗様の宮殿（くうでん）2基は永正5年（1508年）建立の記録がある。中世にさかのぼる修験道建築の稀少な遺例として貴重である。文化庁監修『解説版新指定重要文化財 11 建造物I』（毎日新聞社、1981）、p.74 image:P8220538_Okusha_1.JPG|奥社本殿 image:P8220543_Okusha_2.JPG|奥社本殿南面 ; 山号は小菅山。桜本坊。元隆寺別当大聖院の堂舎。享保年間に法印俊栄によって中興開基されたと伝えられる、[[真言宗]]寺院。神仏分離以後、大聖院別当は神職となり、仏教に関する什器は菩提院に移されている。信濃三十三箇所霊場第十九番札所。 ; 護摩堂 : 小菅山元隆寺別当大聖院の跡地。現存する堂舎は、[[寛延]]3年（[[1750]]）に再建されたもの。 == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (はしらまつさいとうしんじ) is the principal ritual of Kosuge Shrine (小菅神社), which was formerly held annually on July 15. Currently, it is conducted once every three years on a Sunday in mid-July. It is also known as Matsuko. It is designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}} (designated as "Kosuge's Hashiramatsu Ritual"). In the plaza in front of the Kosuge Shrine Satomiya Lecture Hall (里宮講堂), two pillar pines, each 4 meters tall and bound together with assorted wood tied with straw, are erected. A figure known as Matsukamiko (松神子) ascends these two pillars, and the speed with which it ignites them using flint and steel is contested. It is said that if the eastern pillar triumphs, it portends universal peace, whereas if the western pillar wins, it is an omen for a bountiful harvest. This test, originally performed by Shugendō practitioners in conjunction with prayers for abundant crops, is said to have been passed down to the present. Along with {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}} and {{ill|Iinawa Mountain|ja|飯縄山|lt=Iitsuna|lt_ja=飯綱}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Ozunu|ja|役小角}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治時代}} due to the {{ill|Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|ja|神仏分離}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre‑modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. However, according to several ancient documents that recount the shrine’s history, the Shugendō temple Ganryūji (元隆寺), founded by En no Ozunu, is considered the origin of Kosugeyama. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Horse-Headed Kannon|ja|馬頭観音}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. En no Ozunu subsequently enshrined Kosuge Gongen as the principal deity and, in addition, invited and enshrined seven deities—{{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|lt=Kumano|lt_ja=熊野}}, {{ill|Kanminesanjin|ja|金峯山寺|lt=Kanminesanjin|lt_ja=金峯山}} ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野}}), {{ill|Hakusan|ja|白山}}, {{ill|Tateyama|ja|立山}}, Sannō, Hayayuki, and {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}}—as shown in Table 1. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文}} ({{ill|1542|ja|1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō Era|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|lt_ja=大同}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|lt=Sengoku period|lt_ja=戦国時代}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji Era|ja|弘治 (日本)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=弘治}} ({{ill|1557|ja|1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku}} ({{ill|1567|ja|1567}}) and the {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō Era|ja|慶長}} (around {{ill|1600|ja|1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5年〈1600年〉/{{ill|Genroku Era|ja|元禄|lt=Genroku|lt_ja=元年}} 〈{{ill|1688|ja|1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:小菅神社]] == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. Table 2 shows the major historical sources related to Kosugeyama. understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:歴史]] === 先史時代 === 他の修験霊場にも見られるように、小菅山にもまた自然信仰の層を見出すことができ、そうした基層をまず見ておくべきであろう。小菅山のある飯山市小菅集落の周辺では、[[縄文時代]]にさかのぼる集落遺跡が発見されており、[[弥生時代]]中期には稲作が開始されていたことが判明している。すなわち、早い時期から小菅山の一帯には定住が見られたのである。すぐ北に[[越後国]]をひかえた、世界でも有数の豪雪地帯でありながら、そうした定住が可能であったのは、雪と森、そしてそれらがもたらす豊かな水のゆえであった。そして修験入山以前の時代には、そうした自然の実り豊かさに対する信仰（水分神信仰）が行われていたことが分かっている。 === 小菅山の確立 === こうした自然信仰的な基層に対し、小菅山の信仰に社寺としての形態が与えられた年代、すなわち小菅山の歴史的創建は、おそくとも[[平安時代]]後期までのことと考えられている。小菅山にまつわる諸史資料のなかで、社伝の木造馬頭観世音菩薩坐像が平安時代後期の作と推定されるためである。 平安時代後期はまた、[[本地垂迹]]思想の定着と、中世熊野御幸の隆盛期でもある。小菅山を含めた北信州一帯においても、[[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|後白河院]]撰の『[[梁塵秘抄]]』に戸隠山がうたわれていることから推測されるように、熊野修験が入り込んできただけでなく、小菅山の確立に寄与したものと考えられている。事実、小菅山を含む小菅荘一帯には、八所権現だけでなく、熊野社も数多く勧請されており、小菅山の霊場としての確立期に熊野修験の活動があったことを知ることができる。 なお、この時期までに小菅山が確立していたことを伝える史料に、社伝の菩提院曼荼羅がある。菩提院曼荼羅は、中国から輸入された絹地に畿内で彩色されたものであり、制作年代は鎌倉時代末期から[[南北朝時代 (日本)|南北朝時代]]にかけてと推定されている。このような希少品を蔵することからも、小菅山が一定の勢力をともなって確立したことをうかがい知ることができるだろう。 === 南北朝時代から隆盛期まで === [[鎌倉幕府]]崩壊から南北朝時代の始まりころまでには、小菅山を含む[[小菅荘]]一帯は、南に[[高梨氏]]勢力下の[[犬飼荘]]、北に[[市河氏]]の[[志久見郷湯山荘]]に接し、両者の緩衝地帯として戦略的な要地となっていた。しかし、南北朝の騒乱はついにこの地に及び、[[延文]]元年（[[1356]]、南朝[[Shōhei]]11年）には、志久見郷侵攻を企てた南朝党の高梨氏が逆撃を受けて小菅にて惨敗している。その後、高梨氏は勢力を盛り返し、市河氏に対する復仇戦に勝利を収めているが、この頃を境に南朝党の勢力は衰微し、両朝統一の趨勢に従った。以後、Ashikaga Shogunateの支配が安定すると共に、小菅山は修験霊場としての隆盛期を迎えることになる。 [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|加耶吉利堂跡]] この頃の小菅山の隆盛を示すものとして、この時期に行われた元隆寺での造営を伝える文書がある。[[応永]]13年（[[1422]]）には、加耶吉利堂が建立され、堂内には近隣の土豪らによって著色観音三十三身板絵（応永年間在銘）が寄進された。[[永享]]2年（[[1430]]）からは4年の歳月をかけて、元隆寺の宮社坊中寺観が再建された。[[永正]]5年（[[1508]]）9月には、奥社内の宮殿が建立され、天文15年（[[1546]]）には、桐竹鳳凰文透彫奥社脇立二面が製作されている。これらの記録からすると、16世紀の半ばまで、小菅山では造営が営々と続けられており、それを可能にするだけの繁栄があったのである。 なお、応永12年（[[1421]]）には、将軍[[足利義持]]が大納言法印忠意に[[禅林寺 (京都市)|禅林寺]]永観堂若王子別当職などとともに、社領として信濃国小菅荘ほかを安堵したとの記録が残されている『信濃史料』第7巻。。この件に関する資料の大半を蔵する禅林寺若王子社は、もともと[[Emperor Go-Shirakawa|後白河院]]が[[永暦]]年間に熊野三山の土を運んで熊野権現を勧請したと伝えられる社である。若王子社領として領知されたことを述べるこの文書から、この時期までに小菅山が京都の支配下におかれていたことが確認できる。[[応仁]]元年（[[1467]]）にも将軍[[足利義政]]から大納言法印忠雅に同様の領知があった『信濃史料』第8巻。。 === 戦国時代 === 戦国時代における信濃は[[上杉氏]]と[[武田氏]]の争覇の舞台であり、その騒乱から小菅山も逃れることはできなかった。実際、既述の謙信願文は、上杉謙信が[[Takeda Shingen|武田晴信]]に合戦を挑むに際してのものである。上杉氏と武田氏の一連の戦いで、小菅山を含む[[小菅集落 (飯山市)|小菅荘]]一帯も戦禍に巻き込まれたことは間違いなく、武田氏領に帰した時期があったのも事実である。とはいえ、略縁起が伝えるように武田氏の侵攻によって一挙に荒廃したとするのは過度な誇張である。武田領となった後、[[天正]]7年（[[1579]]）2月25日付で、武田勝頼は「小菅」と越後赤沢の間の連絡の便を図るため、人家を置かせており、小菅の地の戦略的・交通的な重要性は依然として認知されていたからである。 この時期はまた、京都からの自立の時期でもあったようである。永禄11年（[[1567]]）の禅林寺若王子神社領覚書『信濃史料』第13巻。によれば、小菅荘からの年貢が不達である旨が述べられており、この頃までには京都の支配から脱していたことが推定される。 [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|護摩堂（大聖院跡）]] === 近世以降の小菅 === その後、天正10年（[[1582]]）3月に織田・徳川連合軍の武田領侵攻により武田氏が滅亡し、川中島四郡は[[織田氏]]の家臣・[[森長可]]が支配する。同年6月の[[本能寺の変]]により「[[天正壬午の乱]]」が発生すると、小菅は越後国の[[上杉景勝]]領となり、情勢が安定を見るとともに奥社本殿が再建された。 再建にあたっては、小菅山の経営にあたっていた別当寺院大聖院のほか、18坊が願主となり、天正19年（[[1591]]）に完成している。完成の2年後、[[文禄]]2年（[[1593]]）には、[[越後国|越後]]の人、金丸与八郎が鉄製鰐口を奉納している「小菅神社所蔵棟札銘写」および「小菅神社所蔵鉄製鰐口」、いずれも『信濃史料』第17巻所収。。この様に、度重なる混乱に巻き込まれながらも、越後からの鰐口奉納があったことに見られるように、小菅の宗教的権威は依然として衰えなかった。 慶長3年（[[1598]]）2月、上杉氏の会津移封にともなって大聖院が移転した。このことにより、小菅山の再建が頓挫したとされるが、それは必ずしも正しくない。慶長11年（[[1606]]）には、皆川氏より絵馬2面が寄進されており、大聖院の移転と小菅山の聖地としての性格は別個のものであった。また、新たな別当に神袋坊を迎えて大聖院自体も存続しているのである。

大聖院の移転が小菅の退勢をもたらさなかったことを裏付けるものとして、大聖院と小菅村の石高記録がある（表3）。文禄4年（[[1594]]）に実施された上杉領内検地の記録『文禄三年上納員数録』によれば、大聖院の知行高は58石とされ、小菅の集落全体を下回る。以後、近世の記録を見ても、小菅の石高と大聖院の知行高には開きがあることが分かる。しばしば大聖院と小菅は同一視され、大聖院が小菅に及ぼした影響力ないし支配力は非常に大きなものと見なされる。しかし、上記のような石高記録が示すところによれば、実際には大聖院は小菅の一部であったのである。 大聖院が小菅の一部であったという論点はさらに、小菅神社の主要な神事である[[#柱松柴灯神事|柱松柴灯神事]]の形態によっても補強されるだろう。 [[image:P8220504_Satosha_hall.JPG|thumb|right|250px|里宮講堂。講堂の前庭で柱松柴灯神事が行われる。]] 柱松柴灯神事は修験道の祭事とされ、元隆寺が大きな役割を担ったとされてきた。しかし、略縁起やそれに由来する通説的理解の説くところによれば、元隆寺は戦国期の荒廃以後、再建されることもなく荒廃するにまかされて、[[江戸時代|近世]]にさしかかる[[17世紀]]初めには、すでに廃墟と化していたのではなかったのだろうか。戦国期に元隆寺が衰退したままであったのならば、なぜ柱松柴灯神事のような大きな祭事を執行・維持できたのかが説明できない。また、寺院が主導したというならば、[[明治]]期の廃仏毀釈にもかかわらず、祭が廃絶しなかったのかを説明できない。さらに、諸史料に見られる柱松柴灯神事の記述を追ってみると、「修験神輿前において柱松柴灯護摩を修す」（来由記）、（奥院にて）「馬頭の護摩を修す」「天下太平のために奥院におゐて長日の護摩を始終す」（略縁起）などとあり、修験寺院の祭事としての性格が明瞭である。それにもかかわらず、今日の柱松柴灯神事には護摩にかかわる儀礼は存在しておらず、寺院による関与も見られないのである。今日の神事に用いられる山伏面・山姥面が江戸時代初期に製作されていることや、奥社参道の杉並木や小菅に残されている宗教建築の多くが江戸時代に整備されたものであることが判明しており、その様に積極的な霊場経営が行われていたという事実は、通説的理解と整合しない。以上のように、通説的理解はいくつもの矛盾を含んでいるのである。 そうした通説的理解とは異なる小菅の近世の姿を描き出している点で、注目すべき民俗史料がある。[[天明]]3年（[[1783]]）に取り決められた「御祭禮日市中村定連判帳」である。この文書は、祭礼日の治安維持や、参詣者を目当てにした市の管理、市に出店する店からの金銭徴収などが定められており、要約するならば里人による祭礼運営の規約である。この文書が示すところからすると、祭礼に出店する商人たちからの金銭徴収は村の収入となっていた。そのため、市を栄させるために必要な配慮がなされており、そのあらわれがこの文書である。このことが示すところは、祭礼が小菅の村の世俗的運営に委ねられていたということに他ならない。 以上からすると、中世から近世への移行期にあって、霊場としての小菅の統治は、領主の庇護下にある寺院の手から里人の手に移り、それとともに祭礼の性格も宗教的なものから、観客（参詣者）に見せることに重きを置いた愉楽的・観光的な性格に移行して行ったと考えられる。そして、そのために、明治の廃仏毀釈を経ても柱松神事は途絶えることがなかったのである。 小菅山の歴史についての通説的理解は、元隆寺やその別当寺院たる大聖院の役割を非常に大きなものとして描いてきた。しかしながら、そうした通説的理解が正しくないことが、以上から浮かび上がってくる。戦国期の兵乱を経てもなお、元隆寺の勢威は衰えたわけではなかった。しかしながら、近世以降の小菅山においては、里人の世俗的な霊場経営が優越し、元隆寺が霊場経営に果たした役割は逆に縮小して行ったのである。 === 近代 === 明治時代になって、神仏分離令が発されると、小菅山においても小菅神社と大聖院が分離されることとなった。しかし、[[明治]]2年（[[1868]]）には大聖院別当職にあった武内英真が神職に就き、仏式什器を菩提寺に移管する一方で、小菅山八所大権現を小菅社八所と改め、今日の小菅神社の直接的な起源に当たる神社が成立した。 明治3年（[[1871]]）に[[社格#近代社格制度| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|type]]制度がしかれると、小菅神社は、[[1873]]（明治6年）に郷社に列せられ、[[1933]]（昭和8年）には県社に列せられている。[[1909]]（明治42年）には、小菅村内の村社19社と無格社5社を合祀し、[[1946]]（[[昭和]]21年）の分社寺まで、一村の村民全てを氏子とした。[[1951]]（昭和29年）の神道指令までは、例祭日には県の奉幣使の参向があった。 == 小菅神社神域内の文化財 == 小菅山は、自然信仰の時代には水分神が祀られ、後に熊野修験の手によって霊場として確立された。そのため、[[熊野神社|熊野社]]が各所に見られる。来由記などに記されたところによれば、神社結界地となっていたのは、大倉崎口（現在の飯山市大字常盤）、関沢口、前坂口、神戸口の4箇所で、それぞれ鳥居が設けられており、神域への入口となっていた。この結界内部には、小菅神社に由縁ある社寺・史跡・民俗が今日に伝えられている。 ; 奥社本殿（重要文化財） : 小菅神社の本殿。大聖院跡地護摩堂から続く参道をぬけ、溶岩性の岩石が露出する急峻な登山道を進んだ、標高820m付近にある。天正19年（1592年）の修復記録があり、棟札によれば小野源之丞政高なる大工が修造にあたったとある。小菅神社の祭神8柱を祀る。 : 屋根は入母屋造、妻入、銅板葺き。桁行・梁間とも4間（「間」は柱間の数を指す）。柱間を正側面とも偶数とする（中央に柱が来る）のは、社寺建築には珍しい。組物は出三斗（でみつと）、軒は二軒繁垂木（ふたのきしげだるき）とする。東・南・西の3面に切目縁をめぐらし、東面は後方3間分に下屋（げや）を設ける。北面は岩窟が迫っている。南面は斜面に張り出した[[懸造]]とし、西側に階段をつけて西の縁から社殿に上るようになっている。建物は天文年間（1532 - 1554年）の建立とみられ、内部に安置される禅宗様の宮殿（くうでん）2基は永正5年（1508年）建立の記録がある。中世にさかのぼる修験道建築の稀少な遺例として貴重である。文化庁監修『解説版新指定重要文化財 11 建造物I』（毎日新聞社、1981）、p.74 image:P8220538_Okusha_1.JPG|奥社本殿 image:P8220543_Okusha_2.JPG|奥社本殿南面 ; 山号は小菅山。桜本坊。元隆寺別当大聖院の堂舎。享保年間に法印俊栄によって中興開基されたと伝えられる、[[真言宗]]寺院。神仏分離以後、大聖院別当は神職となり、仏教に関する什器は菩提院に移されている。信濃三十三箇所霊場第十九番札所。 ; 護摩堂 : 小菅山元隆寺別当大聖院の跡地。現存する堂舎は、[[寛延]]3年（[[1750]]）に再建されたもの。 == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (はしらまつさいとうしんじ) is the principal ritual of Kosuge Shrine (小菅神社), which was formerly held annually on July 15. Currently, it is conducted once every three years on a Sunday in mid-July. It is also known as Matsuko. It is designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}} (designated as "Kosuge's Hashiramatsu Ritual"). In the plaza in front of the Kosuge Shrine Satomiya Lecture Hall (里宮講堂), two pillar pines, each 4 meters tall and bound together with assorted wood tied with straw, are erected. A figure known as Matsukamiko (松神子) ascends these two pillars, and the speed with which it ignites them using flint and steel is contested. It is said that if the eastern pillar triumphs, it portends universal peace, whereas if the western pillar wins, it is an omen for a bountiful harvest. This test, originally performed by Shugendō practitioners in conjunction with prayers for abundant crops, is said to have been passed down to the present. Along with {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}} and {{ill|Iinawa Mountain|ja|飯縄山|lt=Iitsuna|lt_ja=飯綱}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Ozunu|ja|役小角}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治時代}} due to the {{ill|Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|ja|神仏分離}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre‑modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. However, according to several ancient documents that recount the shrine’s history, the Shugendō temple Ganryūji (元隆寺), founded by En no Ozunu, is considered the origin of Kosugeyama. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Horse-Headed Kannon|ja|馬頭観音}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. En no Ozunu subsequently enshrined Kosuge Gongen as the principal deity and, in addition, invited and enshrined seven deities—{{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|lt=Kumano|lt_ja=熊野}}, {{ill|Kanminesanjin|ja|金峯山寺|lt=Kanminesanjin|lt_ja=金峯山}} ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野}}), {{ill|Hakusan|ja|白山}}, {{ill|Tateyama|ja|立山}}, Sannō, Hayayuki, and {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}}—as shown in Table 1. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文}} ({{ill|1542|ja|1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō Era|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|lt_ja=大同}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|lt=Sengoku period|lt_ja=戦国時代}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji Era|ja|弘治 (日本)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=弘治}} ({{ill|1557|ja|1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku}} ({{ill|1567|ja|1567}}) and the {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō Era|ja|慶長}} (around {{ill|1600|ja|1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5年〈1600年〉/{{ill|Genroku Era|ja|元禄|lt=Genroku|lt_ja=元年}} 〈{{ill|1688|ja|1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:小菅神社]] == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. Table 2 shows the major historical sources related to Kosugeyama. In the descriptions that follow, the abbreviations listed in Table 2 will be used when referring to these sources. {|class="wikitable" |+'''Table 2: List of Major Historical Sources of Kosugeyama''' ! Document Name ! Abbreviation ! Date/Period ! Summary |- ! Record of the Origins of the Kosugeyama Eight Gongen and Ganryūji, Takai District, Shinano Province | Origin Record | Tenmon 11 (1542) | Describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, sacred boundaries, and its historical evolution. It is recorded under the name “別当并衆徒中.” |- ! Nagaoka Kagetora Prayer Document Draft | Kenshin Prayer Document | Kōji 3 (1557) | A prayer document issued as Ganryūji prepared for battle against Takeda Harunobu. It recounts the founding tradition and prosperity of Ganryūji and, while referencing Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, offers prayers for military success. |- ! Illustration of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Illustration of Ganryūji | Eirōku 9 (1666) | An illustration depicting the flourishing state of Kosugeyama in the medieval period, showing Ganryūji accompanied by numerous monastic quarters. The production date is questionableAs an illustration depicting the flourishing period of Kosugeyama, an illustration of Ganryūji bearing the inscription {{ill|1566|ja|1566}} ({{ill|Eiroku|ja|永禄|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=永禄}}9) is known. In this illustration, it is said that there were 19 monastic quarters in the upper complex, 19 in the middle, and 11 in the lower complex, and that the main hall overseeing these—the Daisēin—had 19 subsidiary chapels. However, this illustration contradicts the timeline of the disastrous {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}} in {{ill|1561|ja|1561}} (Eirōku 4) as mentioned earlier. Additionally, the names of the monastic quarters and the positions of the stone walls do not correspond with the dates, raising several doubts. For these reasons, it is possible that this illustration was retrospectively drawn in the early modern period to showcase the prosperity of Kosuge, and its reliability as a historical source should be regarded with caution. [信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ編 2005:76-77]. |- ! Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Brief Origins | Composed in Keichō 5 (1600) and revised in Genroku 1 (1688) | Based on the account in the Origin Record, this document describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, and its historical evolution. It details the flourishing during the medieval period and the subsequent devastation and decline caused by the military fires of the Takeda clan, thereby forming the basis for the conventional understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:歴史]] === Prehistoric Era === Similar to other Shugendō sacred sites, Mount Kosuge (小菅山) also exhibits layers of nature worship which must be acknowledged first. Around the Kosuge settlement in Iiyama city, remains of settlements dating back to the {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}} have been discovered, and it has been confirmed that rice cultivation began by the mid-{{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}. Hence, the area around Mount Kosuge saw early settlement. Despite being one of the snowiest regions in the world adjacent to {{ill|Echigo Province|ja|越後国}} to the north, settlement was possible due to abundant water resources from snow and forests. It is known that prior to Shugendō practices, there was worship related to this abundant natural productivity (water deity worship). === Establishment of Mount Kosuge === The historical establishment of Mount Kosuge as a religious site with shrines and temples is considered to have occurred no later than the late {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}}. This conclusion is drawn from historical artifacts, such as the wooden seated statue of Batō Kannon, presumed to have been created in the late Heian period. The late Heian period also saw the establishment of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} thought and the rise of the medieval Kumano pilgrimage. The area around northern Shinano, including Mount Kosuge, was influenced by Kumano Shugendō, inferred from the mention of Mount Togakushi in the {{ill|Ryōjin Hishō|ja|梁塵秘抄}} compiled by {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|後白河天皇}}. Numerous Kumano shrines were established alongside Hachisho Gongen, confirming Kumano Shugendō's role in establishing Kosuge's sacred area. Further evidence of Kosuge’s establishment by this time is the Bodai-in Mandala, painted in Kinai on Chinese-imported silk, dated from the late Kamakura to the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}. Holding such rare artifacts suggests Mount Kosuge was firmly established with significant influence. === Nanboku-chō Period to Prosperity === By the fall of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉幕府}} and the start of the Nanboku-chō period, Kosuge was strategically located between the forces of the {{ill|Takanashi clan|ja|高梨氏}} in Inukai estate to the south and the {{ill|Ichikawa clan|ja|市河氏}} in Shikumigō Yuyama estate to the north. In 1356, Takanashi forces of the Southern Court were defeated at Kosuge while attacking Shikumigō. The area eventually stabilized under Ashikaga shogunate rule, leading to a prosperous era as a Shugendō sacred site. [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Remains of Kayakiri Hall]] Evidence of this prosperity includes the construction of Kayakiri Hall in 1422, where local lords donated paintings of the Thirty-three Manifestations of Kannon. Extensive rebuilding of Genryū-ji Temple occurred between 1430-1434, and other major constructions continued into the mid-16th century. In 1421, shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi granted Kosuge estate to Daijōin Hōin Chūi along with Wakaoji of {{ill|Zenrin-ji|ja|禅林寺}}, establishing control from Kyoto. A similar grant occurred in 1467 by Ashikaga Yoshimasa, confirming Kosuge’s integration under Kyoto’s influence. === Sengoku Period === During the Sengoku period, Kosuge suffered from conflicts between the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}} and {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}}. Despite temporary Takeda control, strategic importance ensured continuous habitation. By 1567, documents from Zenrin-ji note that Kosuge ceased tribute, indicating independence from Kyoto. [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gomadō (former Daishōin site)]] === Early Modern Period and Later === Post-1582, Kosuge came under {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|ja|上杉景勝}} after the fall of the Takeda. Rebuilding occurred, completed by 1591, demonstrating continued religious influence. Despite Daishōin's relocation to Aizu in 1598, local religious activities persisted, demonstrating Daishōin's lesser influence than commonly perceived. Table 3 illustrates Kosuge's consistent economic vitality, independent from Daishōin's fluctuating status. Furthermore, the secular management of rituals by villagers reinforced Kosuge’s local religious authority. === Modern Era === The Meiji government's Shinto-Buddhist separation saw the transformation of Mount Kosuge into Kosuge Shrine. Established in 1868, it became a village shrine in 1873 and a prefectural shrine in 1933. Local shrines merged in 1909, solidifying Kosuge Shrine’s modern status. == Cultural Properties within Kosuge Shrine == Kosuge Shrine contains significant cultural properties such as the main hall (Important Cultural Property) dating from mid-Muromachi, established around 1532-1554, unique for its architectural design. Other treasures include Niōmon, Satomiya, Bodai-in, and cedar avenues dating from the Edo period, along with remarkable natural and cultural landmarks detailed in Table 4. == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual is Kosuge Shrine’s principal ritual, designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}}. Traditionally held annually, it now occurs every three years in July, involving ceremonial burning of pillar pines to predict peace or harvest prosperity. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:柱松柴灯神事]] == Transportation == * From JR East {{ill|Iiyama Station|ja|飯山駅}} (Iiyama Line), take Nagaden bus towards Nozawa Onsen, alight at Sekizawa stop (25 min), walk 20 min. == References == {{Reflist|2}} == Further Reading == * See original text for references. == See Also == {{Commonscat|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} * {{ill|Mount Togakushi|ja|戸隠山}} * {{ill|Shugendō|ja|修験道}} * {{ill|En no Gyōja|ja|役小角}} * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰}} == External Links == * [http://kosugejinja.jp/ 小菅神社] - 公式サイト * [http://www.janis.or.jp/users/ozunu/ 小菅の里] — 小菅神社が所在する小菅地区の研究・文化財保護・振興にとりくむ「小菅の里保護委員会」の公式サイト。 * [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/bunkazai/bunkazai.htm 飯山市の文化財] — [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/top.htm 飯山市ふるさと館]公式サイト内。地区の欄に瑞穂とあるのが、小菅神社神域内の文化財。種別、写真、登録日付など基礎情報。 * [http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/kosuge.html 小菅神社の里・飯山市] — 地域情報サイト「[http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/ 信州の旅.com]」内コンテンツ。 * [http://www.omiyasan.com/north/iiyama/post-56.php 小菅神社奥社] — 神社情報サイト「[http://www.omiyasan.com/ おみやさんcom]」内コンテンツ。 * 2万5千分の1 地形図「[http://watchizu.gsi.go.jp/watchizu.html?b=365346&l=1382607 往郷]」 — 国土地理院・[https://maps.gsi.go.jp/ 地図閲覧サービス]。 {{Normdaten}} {{citation needed|こすけしんしや いいやまし}} [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の旧県社]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の神社]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:Gongen]][[Category:神仏習合]] [[Category:Shinto-Buddhist syncretism]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:役小角]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:修験道]] [[Category:Shugendo]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:真言系仏教]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:信濃三十三観音霊場]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:重要文化財 (建造物)]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の重要文化財]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:飯山市の歴史]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:飯山市の建築物]] [[Category:Pages to be translated]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[ja:小菅神社 (飯山市)]][[category:kk]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:Mass editing to refresh the first new Wikipedia redirects]] [[sn:osuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] {{DEFAULTSORT:Kosuge Shrine (Iiyama)}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Kosuge Shrine (Iiyama)}}

Former {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社}} (1933) |Founding = Unknown |Main hall = Irimoya style |religious_affiliation = {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}|festival = Sunday in mid-July |Ritual = Hashiramatsu Shibatō Ritual (every three years) |Map = {{location map+|Japan Nagano|width=210|float=center|caption=|places= {{location map~|Japan Nagano|lat_deg=36|lat_min=53|lat_sec=46.2|lon_deg=138|lon_min=25|lon_sec=21.3|position=left|label=Satomiya|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{location map~|Japan Nagano|lat_deg=36|lat_min=53|lat_sec=47.6|lon_deg=138|lon_min=26|lon_sec=7.4|position=right|label=Inner Shrine|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}}}} {{OSM location map|coord={{coord|36.895701|N|138.415382|E}}|fullscreen-option=0|zoom=11|float=center|width=200|caption=|title=|mark-coord1={{coord|36|53|46.2|N|138|25|21.3|E}}|label1=Satomiya|label-pos1=left|mark-size1=8|mark-coord2={{coord|36|53|47.6|N|138|26|7.4|E}}|label2=Inner Shrine|label-pos2=right|mark-size2=8}} }} '''Kosuge Shrine (小菅神社)''' is a {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|ja|長野県}} {{ill|Iiyama|ja|飯山市}}-based {{ill|Shinto Shrine|ja|神社}}. Along with {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}} and {{ill|Iinawa Mountain|ja|飯縄山|lt=Iitsuna|lt_ja=飯綱}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Ozunu|ja|役小角}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治時代}} due to the {{ill|Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|ja|神仏分離}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre‑modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文}} ({{ill|1542|ja|1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō Era|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|lt_ja=大同}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|lt=Sengoku period|lt_ja=戦国時代}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji Era|ja|弘治 (日本)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=弘治}} ({{ill|1557|ja|1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku}} ({{ill|1567|ja|1567}}) and the {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō Era|ja|慶長}} (around {{ill|1600|ja|1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5年〈1600年〉/{{ill|Genroku Era|ja|元禄|lt=Genroku|lt_ja=元年}} 〈{{ill|1688|ja|1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:小菅神社]] == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. Table 2 shows the major historical sources related to Kosugeyama. In the descriptions that follow, the abbreviations listed in Table 2 will be used when referring to these sources. {|class="wikitable" |+'''Table 2: List of Major Historical Sources of Kosugeyama''' ! Document Name ! Abbreviation ! Date/Period ! Summary |- ! Record of the Origins of the Kosugeyama Eight Gongen and Ganryūji, Takai District, Shinano Province | Origin Record | Tenmon 11 (1542) | Describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, sacred boundaries, and its historical evolution. It is recorded under the name “別当并衆徒中.” |- ! Nagaoka Kagetora Prayer Document Draft | Kenshin Prayer Document | Kōji 3 (1557) | A prayer document issued as Ganryūji prepared for battle against Takeda Harunobu. It recounts the founding tradition and prosperity of Ganryūji and, while referencing Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, offers prayers for military success. |- ! Illustration of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Illustration of Ganryūji | Eirōku 9 (1666) | An illustration depicting the flourishing state of Kosugeyama in the medieval period, showing Ganryūji accompanied by numerous monastic quarters. The production date is questionableAs an illustration depicting the flourishing period of Kosugeyama, an illustration of Ganryūji bearing the inscription {{ill|1566|ja|1566}} ({{ill|Eiroku|ja|永禄|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=永禄}}9) is known. In this illustration, it is said that there were 19 monastic quarters in the upper complex, 19 in the middle, and 11 in the lower complex, and that the main hall overseeing these—the Daisēin—had 19 subsidiary chapels. However, this illustration contradicts the timeline of the disastrous {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}} in {{ill|1561|ja|1561}} (Eirōku 4) as mentioned earlier. Additionally, the names of the monastic quarters and the positions of the stone walls do not correspond with the dates, raising several doubts. For these reasons, it is possible that this illustration was retrospectively drawn in the early modern period to showcase the prosperity of Kosuge, and its reliability as a historical source should be regarded with caution. [信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ編 2005:76-77]. |- ! Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Brief Origins | Composed in Keichō 5 (1600) and revised in Genroku 1 (1688) | Based on the account in the Origin Record, this document describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, and its historical evolution. It details the flourishing during the medieval period and the subsequent devastation and decline caused by the military fires of the Takeda clan, thereby forming the basis for the conventional understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:歴史]] === Prehistoric Era === Similar to other Shugendō sacred sites, Mount Kosuge (小菅山) also exhibits layers of nature worship which must be acknowledged first. Around the Kosuge settlement in Iiyama city, remains of settlements dating back to the {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}} have been discovered, and it has been confirmed that rice cultivation began by the mid-{{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}. Hence, the area around Mount Kosuge saw early settlement. Despite being one of the snowiest regions in the world adjacent to {{ill|Echigo Province|ja|越後国}} to the north, settlement was possible due to abundant water resources from snow and forests. It is known that prior to Shugendō practices, there was worship related to this abundant natural productivity (water deity worship). === Establishment of Mount Kosuge === The historical establishment of Mount Kosuge as a religious site with shrines and temples is considered to have occurred no later than the late {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}}. This conclusion is drawn from historical artifacts, such as the wooden seated statue of Batō Kannon, presumed to have been created in the late Heian period. The late Heian period also saw the establishment of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} thought and the rise of the medieval Kumano pilgrimage. The area around northern Shinano, including Mount Kosuge, was influenced by Kumano Shugendō, inferred from the mention of Mount Togakushi in the {{ill|Ryōjin Hishō|ja|梁塵秘抄}} compiled by {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|後白河天皇}}. Numerous Kumano shrines were established alongside Hachisho Gongen, confirming Kumano Shugendō's role in establishing Kosuge's sacred area. Further evidence of Kosuge’s establishment by this time is the Bodai-in Mandala, painted in Kinai on Chinese-imported silk, dated from the late Kamakura to the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}. Holding such rare artifacts suggests Mount Kosuge was firmly established with significant influence. === Nanboku-chō Period to Prosperity === By the fall of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉幕府}} and the start of the Nanboku-chō period, Kosuge was strategically located between the forces of the {{ill|Takanashi clan|ja|高梨氏}} in Inukai estate to the south and the {{ill|Ichikawa clan|ja|市河氏}} in Shikumigō Yuyama estate to the north. In 1356, Takanashi forces of the Southern Court were defeated at Kosuge while attacking Shikumigō. The area eventually stabilized under Ashikaga shogunate rule, leading to a prosperous era as a Shugendō sacred site. [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Remains of Kayakiri Hall]] Evidence of this prosperity includes the construction of Kayakiri Hall in 1422, where local lords donated paintings of the Thirty-three Manifestations of Kannon. Extensive rebuilding of Genryū-ji Temple occurred between 1430-1434, and other major constructions continued into the mid-16th century. In 1421, shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi granted Kosuge estate to Daijōin Hōin Chūi along with Wakaoji of {{ill|Zenrin-ji|ja|禅林寺}}, establishing control from Kyoto. A similar grant occurred in 1467 by Ashikaga Yoshimasa, confirming Kosuge’s integration under Kyoto’s influence. === Sengoku Period === During the Sengoku period, Kosuge suffered from conflicts between the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}} and {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}}. Despite temporary Takeda control, strategic importance ensured continuous habitation. By 1567, documents from Zenrin-ji note that Kosuge ceased tribute, indicating independence from Kyoto. [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gomadō (former Daishōin site)]] === Early Modern Period and Later === Post-1582, Kosuge came under {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|ja|上杉景勝}} after the fall of the Takeda. Rebuilding occurred, completed by 1591, demonstrating continued religious influence. Despite Daishōin's relocation to Aizu in 1598, local religious activities persisted, demonstrating Daishōin's lesser influence than commonly perceived. Table 3 illustrates Kosuge's consistent economic vitality, independent from Daishōin's fluctuating status. Furthermore, the secular management of rituals by villagers reinforced Kosuge’s local religious authority. === Modern Era === The Meiji government's Shinto-Buddhist separation saw the transformation of Mount Kosuge into Kosuge Shrine. Established in 1868, it became a village shrine in 1873 and a prefectural shrine in 1933. Local shrines merged in 1909, solidifying Kosuge Shrine’s modern status. == Cultural Properties within Kosuge Shrine == Kosuge Shrine contains significant cultural properties such as the main hall (Important Cultural Property) dating from mid-Muromachi, established around 1532-1554, unique for its architectural design. Other treasures include Niōmon, Satomiya, Bodai-in, and cedar avenues dating from the Edo period, along with remarkable natural and cultural landmarks detailed in Table 4. == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual is Kosuge Shrine’s principal ritual, designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}}. Traditionally held annually, it now occurs every three years in July, involving ceremonial burning of pillar pines to predict peace or harvest prosperity. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:柱松柴灯神事]] == Transportation == * From JR East {{ill|Iiyama Station|ja|飯山駅}} (Iiyama Line), take Nagaden bus towards Nozawa Onsen, alight at Sekizawa stop (25 min), walk 20 min. == References == {{Reflist|2}} == Further Reading == * See original text for references. == See Also == {{Commonscat|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} * {{ill|Mount Togakushi|ja|戸隠山}} * {{ill|Shugendō|ja|修験道}} * {{ill|En no Gyōja|ja|役小角}} * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰}} == External Links == * [http://kosugejinja.jp/ 小菅神社] - 公式サイト * [http://www.janis.or.jp/users/ozunu/ 小菅の里] — 小菅神社が所在する小菅地区の研究・文化財保護・振興にとりくむ「小菅の里保護委員会」の公式サイト。 * [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/bunkazai/bunkazai.htm 飯山市の文化財] — [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/top.htm 飯山市ふるさと館]公式サイト内。地区の欄に瑞穂とあるのが、小菅神社神域内の文化財。種別、写真、登録日付など基礎情報。 * [http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/kosuge.html 小菅神社の里・飯山市] — 地域情報サイト「[http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/ 信州の旅.com]」内コンテンツ。 * [http://www.omiyasan.com/north/iiyama/post-56.php 小菅神社奥社] — 神社情報サイト「[http://www.omiyasan.com/ おみやさんcom]」内コンテンツ。 * 2万5千分の1 地形図「[http://watchizu.gsi.go.jp/watchizu.html?b=365346&l=1382607 往郷]」 — 国土地理院・[https://maps.gsi.go.jp/ 地図閲覧サービス]。 {{Normdaten}} {{citation needed|こすけしんしや いいやまし}} [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の旧県社]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の神社]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:Gongen]][[Category:神仏習合]] [[Category:Shinto-Buddhist syncretism]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:役小角]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:修験道]] [[Category:Shugendo]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:真言系仏教]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:信濃三十三観音霊場]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:重要文化財 (建造物)]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の重要文化財]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:飯山市の歴史]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:飯山市の建築物]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[ja:小菅神社 (飯山市)]][[category:kk]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:Mass editing to refresh the first new Wikipedia redirects]] [[sn:osuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] {{DEFAULTSORT:Kosuge Shrine (Iiyama)}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Kosuge Shrine (Iiyama)}}

Along with {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}} and {{ill|Iinawa Mountain|ja|飯縄山|lt=Iitsuna|lt_ja=飯綱}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Ozunu|ja|役小角}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治時代}} due to the {{ill|Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|ja|神仏分離}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre‑modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Horse-Headed Kannon|ja|馬頭観音}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. In this illustration, it is said that there were 19 monastic quarters in the upper complex, 19 in the middle, and 11 in the lower complex, and that the main hall overseeing these—the Daisēin—had 19 subsidiary chapels. However, this illustration contradicts the timeline of the disastrous {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}} in {{ill|1561|ja|1561}} (Eirōku 4) as mentioned earlier. It details the flourishing during the medieval period and the subsequent devastation and decline caused by the military fires of the Takeda clan, thereby forming the basis for the conventional understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:歴史]] === Prehistoric Era === Similar to other Shugendō sacred sites, Mount Kosuge (小菅山) also exhibits layers of nature worship which must be acknowledged first. Around the Kosuge settlement in Iiyama city, remains of settlements dating back to the {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}} have been discovered, and it has been confirmed that rice cultivation began by the mid-{{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}. Hence, the area around Mount Kosuge saw early settlement. Despite being one of the snowiest regions in the world adjacent to {{ill|Echigo Province|ja|越後国}} to the north, settlement was possible due to abundant water resources from snow and forests. It is known that prior to Shugendō practices, there was worship related to this abundant natural productivity (water deity worship). === Establishment of Mount Kosuge === The historical establishment of Mount Kosuge as a religious site with shrines and temples is considered to have occurred no later than the late {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代}}. This conclusion is drawn from historical artifacts, such as the wooden seated statue of Batō Kannon, presumed to have been created in the late Heian period. The late Heian period also saw the establishment of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} thought and the rise of the medieval Kumano pilgrimage. The area around northern Shinano, including Mount Kosuge, was influenced by Kumano Shugendō, inferred from the mention of Mount Togakushi in the {{ill|Ryōjin Hishō|ja|梁塵秘抄}} compiled by {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|ja|後白河天皇}}. Numerous Kumano shrines were established alongside Hachisho Gongen, confirming Kumano Shugendō's role in establishing Kosuge's sacred area. Further evidence of Kosuge’s establishment by this time is the Bodai-in Mandala, painted in Kinai on Chinese-imported silk, dated from the late Kamakura to the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}. Holding such rare artifacts suggests Mount Kosuge was firmly established with significant influence. === Nanboku-chō Period to Prosperity === By the fall of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉幕府}} and the start of the Nanboku-chō period, Kosuge was strategically located between the forces of the {{ill|Takanashi clan|ja|高梨氏}} in Inukai estate to the south and the {{ill|Ichikawa clan|ja|市河氏}} in Shikumigō Yuyama estate to the north. In 1356, Takanashi forces of the Southern Court were defeated at Kosuge while attacking Shikumigō. The area eventually stabilized under Ashikaga shogunate rule, leading to a prosperous era as a Shugendō sacred site. [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Remains of Kayakiri Hall]] Evidence of this prosperity includes the construction of Kayakiri Hall in 1422, where local lords donated paintings of the Thirty-three Manifestations of Kannon. Extensive rebuilding of Genryū-ji Temple occurred between 1430-1434, and other major constructions continued into the mid-16th century. In 1421, shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi granted Kosuge estate to Daijōin Hōin Chūi along with Wakaoji of {{ill|Zenrin-ji|ja|禅林寺}}, establishing control from Kyoto. A similar grant occurred in 1467 by Ashikaga Yoshimasa, confirming Kosuge’s integration under Kyoto’s influence. === Sengoku Period === During the Sengoku period, Kosuge suffered from conflicts between the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}} and {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}}. Despite temporary Takeda control, strategic importance ensured continuous habitation. By 1567, documents from Zenrin-ji note that Kosuge ceased tribute, indicating independence from Kyoto. [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gomadō (former Daishōin site)]] === Early Modern Period and Later === Post-1582, Kosuge came under {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|ja|上杉景勝}} after the fall of the Takeda. Rebuilding occurred, completed by 1591, demonstrating continued religious influence. Despite Daishōin's relocation to Aizu in 1598, local religious activities persisted, demonstrating Daishōin's lesser influence than commonly perceived. Table 3 illustrates Kosuge's consistent economic vitality, independent from Daishōin's fluctuating status. Furthermore, the secular management of rituals by villagers reinforced Kosuge’s local religious authority. === Modern Era === The Meiji government's Shinto-Buddhist separation saw the transformation of Mount Kosuge into Kosuge Shrine. Established in 1868, it became a village shrine in 1873 and a prefectural shrine in 1933. Local shrines merged in 1909, solidifying Kosuge Shrine’s modern status. == Cultural Properties within Kosuge Shrine == Kosuge Shrine contains significant cultural properties such as the main hall (Important Cultural Property) dating from mid-Muromachi, established around 1532-1554, unique for its architectural design. Other treasures include Niōmon, Satomiya, Bodai-in, and cedar avenues dating from the Edo period, along with remarkable natural and cultural landmarks detailed in Table 4. == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual is Kosuge Shrine’s principal ritual, designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}}. Traditionally held annually, it now occurs every three years in July, involving ceremonial burning of pillar pines to predict peace or harvest prosperity. Along with {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}} and {{ill|Iinawa Mountain|ja|飯縄山|lt=Iitsuna|lt_ja=飯綱}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Ozunu|ja|役小角}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治時代}} due to the {{ill|Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|ja|神仏分離}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre‑modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. However, according to several ancient documents that recount the shrine’s history, the Shugendō temple Ganryūji (元隆寺), founded by En no Ozunu, is considered the origin of Kosugeyama. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Horse-Headed Kannon|ja|馬頭観音}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. En no Ozunu subsequently enshrined Kosuge Gongen as the principal deity and, in addition, invited and enshrined seven deities—{{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|lt=Kumano|lt_ja=熊野}}, {{ill|Kanminesanjin|ja|金峯山寺|lt=Kanminesanjin|lt_ja=金峯山}} ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野}}), {{ill|Hakusan|ja|白山}}, {{ill|Tateyama|ja|立山}}, Sannō, Hayayuki, and {{ill|Togakushi Mountain|ja|戸隠山|lt=Togakushi|lt_ja=戸隠}}—as shown in Table 1. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文}} ({{ill|1542|ja|1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō Era|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|lt_ja=大同}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|lt=Sengoku period|lt_ja=戦国時代}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji Era|ja|弘治 (日本)|lt=Kōji|lt_ja=弘治}} ({{ill|1557|ja|1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku}} ({{ill|1567|ja|1567}}) and the {{ill|Battle of Kawanakajima|ja|川中島の戦い}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō Era|ja|慶長}} (around {{ill|1600|ja|1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5年〈1600年〉/{{ill|Genroku Era|ja|元禄|lt=Genroku|lt_ja=元年}} 〈{{ill|1688|ja|1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:小菅神社]] == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. In 1356, Takanashi forces of the Southern Court were defeated at Kosuge while attacking Shikumigō. The area eventually stabilized under Ashikaga shogunate rule, leading to a prosperous era as a Shugendō sacred site. [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Remains of Kayakiri Hall]] Evidence of this prosperity includes the construction of Kayakiri Hall in 1422, where local lords donated paintings of the Thirty-three Manifestations of Kannon. Extensive rebuilding of Genryū-ji Temple occurred between 1430-1434, and other major constructions continued into the mid-16th century. In 1421, shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi granted Kosuge estate to Daijōin Hōin Chūi along with Wakaoji of {{ill|Zenrin-ji|ja|禅林寺}}, establishing control from Kyoto. A similar grant occurred in 1467 by Ashikaga Yoshimasa, confirming Kosuge’s integration under Kyoto’s influence. === Sengoku Period === During the Sengoku period, Kosuge suffered from conflicts between the {{ill|Uesugi clan|ja|上杉氏}} and {{ill|Takeda clan|ja|武田氏}}. Despite temporary Takeda control, strategic importance ensured continuous habitation. By 1567, documents from Zenrin-ji note that Kosuge ceased tribute, indicating independence from Kyoto. [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gomadō (former Daishōin site)]] === Early Modern Period and Later === Post-1582, Kosuge came under {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|ja|上杉景勝}} after the fall of the Takeda. Rebuilding occurred, completed by 1591, demonstrating continued religious influence. Despite Daishōin's relocation to Aizu in 1598, local religious activities persisted, demonstrating Daishōin's lesser influence than commonly perceived. Table 3 illustrates Kosuge's consistent economic vitality, independent from Daishōin's fluctuating status. Furthermore, the secular management of rituals by villagers reinforced Kosuge’s local religious authority. === Modern Era === The Meiji government's Shinto-Buddhist separation saw the transformation of Mount Kosuge into Kosuge Shrine. Established in 1868, it became a village shrine in 1873 and a prefectural shrine in 1933. Local shrines merged in 1909, solidifying Kosuge Shrine’s modern status. == Cultural Properties within Kosuge Shrine == Kosuge Shrine contains significant cultural properties such as the main hall (Important Cultural Property) dating from mid-Muromachi, established around 1532-1554, unique for its architectural design. Other treasures include Niōmon, Satomiya, Bodai-in, and cedar avenues dating from the Edo period, along with remarkable natural and cultural landmarks detailed in Table 4. == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual is Kosuge Shrine’s principal ritual, designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}}. Traditionally held annually, it now occurs every three years in July, involving ceremonial burning of pillar pines to predict peace or harvest prosperity. [[Category:Translated pages]][[ja:柱松柴灯神事]] == Transportation == * From JR East {{ill|Iiyama Station|ja|飯山駅}} (Iiyama Line), take Nagaden bus towards Nozawa Onsen, alight at Sekizawa stop (25 min), walk 20 min. == References == {{Reflist|2}} == Further Reading == * See original text for references. == See Also == {{Commonscat|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} * {{ill|Mount Togakushi|ja|戸隠山}} * {{ill|Shugendō|ja|修験道}} * {{ill|En no Gyōja|ja|役小角}} * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰}} == External Links == * [http://kosugejinja.jp/ 小菅神社] - 公式サイト * [http://www.janis.or.jp/users/ozunu/ 小菅の里] — 小菅神社が所在する小菅地区の研究・文化財保護・振興にとりくむ「小菅の里保護委員会」の公式サイト。 * [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/bunkazai/bunkazai.htm 飯山市の文化財] — [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/top.htm 飯山市ふるさと館]公式サイト内。地区の欄に瑞穂とあるのが、小菅神社神域内の文化財。種別、写真、登録日付など基礎情報。 * [http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/kosuge.html 小菅神社の里・飯山市] — 地域情報サイト「[http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/ 信州の旅.com]」内コンテンツ。 * [http://www.omiyasan.com/north/iiyama/post-56.php 小菅神社奥社] — 神社情報サイト「[http://www.omiyasan.com/ おみやさんcom]」内コンテンツ。 * 2万5千分の1 地形図「[http://watchizu.gsi.go.jp/watchizu.html?b=365346&l=1382607 往郷]」 — 国土地理院・[https://maps.gsi.go.jp/ 地図閲覧サービス]。 {{Normdaten}} {{citation needed|こすけしんしや いいやまし}} [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の旧県社]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の神社]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:Gongen]][[Category:神仏習合]] [[Category:Shinto-Buddhist syncretism]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:役小角]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:修験道]] [[Category:Shugendo]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:真言系仏教]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:信濃三十三観音霊場]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:重要文化財 (建造物)]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:長野県の重要文化財]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:飯山市の歴史]] [[Category:Gongen]][[Category:飯山市の建築物]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[ja:小菅神社 (飯山市)]][[category:kk]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:Mass editing to refresh the first new Wikipedia redirects]] [[sn:osuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] [[Category:11]][[sn:Kosuge Shrine (飯山市)]][[Category:11]] {{DEFAULTSORT:Kosuge Shrine (Iiyama)}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Kosuge Shrine (Iiyama)}}
