Local Buddha |- ! {{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=}} ({{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami-no-Mikoto|1=Izanami}}) | {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} | {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|WD=Q236242|lt=Amitabha Buddha|1=Amitābha}} |- ! Konpō Gongen ([[Emperor Ankan]]) | Mount Kanmine ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino|1=Yoshino|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15410122}}) | {{ill|Shakyamuni Tathāgata Buddha|ja|釈迦如来|1=Shakyamuni Tathāgata|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakyamuni Tathāgata Buddha|qq=}} |- ! {{ill|Hakusan Gongen|ja|白山権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakusan Gongen|qq=}} ({{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi-no-Mikoto|1=Izanagi}}) | Hakusan | {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|Ekādaśamukha|WD=Q11404731|lt=Eleven-Faced Kannon|1=Ekādaśamukha}} |- ! {{ill|Tateyama Gongen|ja|立山権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tateyama Gongen|qq=}} ({{ill|Kunitama|en|Kunitama|WD=Q9692242|WD=Q276944|lt=Okuninushi-no-Mikoto|1=Kunitama}}) | Tateyama | {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|WD=Q236242|lt=Amitabha Buddha|1=Amitābha}} |- ! {{ill|Sannō Gongen|ja|山王権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sannō Gongen|comment=enwiki is a redirect|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} ({{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944|WD=Q276944|lt=Okuninushi-no-Mikoto|1=Ōkuninushi}}) | Zao | {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Yakushi Nyorai Medicine Buddha|1=Bhaisajyaguru}} |- ! Togakushi Gongen ({{ill|Ame-no-Tajikarao|en|Ame-no-Tajikarao|WD=Q849412|lt=The Strong-Handed Deity|1=Ame-no-Tajikarao}}) | Togakushi Mountain | {{ill|Āryāvalokiteśvara|ja|聖観音|1=Āryāvalokiteśvara|lt=Shō Kannon|lt_ja=正観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Āryāvalokiteśvara|13=User:Immanuelle/Āryāvalokiteśvara|qq=}} |- ! Kosuge Gongen ({{ill|Matarajin|en|Matarajin|WD=Q6380689|lt=Matarajin|1=Matarajin}}) | (Kosugeyama Main Deity) | {{ill|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|en|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|WD=Q17004306|lt=Horse-Headed Kannon|1=Hayagriva (Buddhism)}} |}
The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. However, according to several ancient documents that recount the shrine’s history, the Shugendō temple Ganryūji (元隆寺), founded by En no Ozunu, is considered the origin of Kosugeyama. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|en|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|WD=Q17004306|lt=Horse-Headed Kannon|1=Hayagriva (Buddhism)}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. En no Ozunu subsequently enshrined Kosuge Gongen as the principal deity and, in addition, invited and enshrined seven deities—{{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|lt=Kumano|lt_ja=熊野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=}}, {{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kanminesanjin|1=Kimpusen-ji}} ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino|1=Yoshino|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15410122}}), {{ill|Mount Haku|en|Mount Haku|WD=Q2639098|lt=Hakusan|1=Mount Haku}}, {{ill|Mount Tate|en|Mount Tate|WD=Q2977103|lt=Tateyama|1=Mount Tate}}, Sannō, Hayayuki, and {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}}—as shown in Table 1. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon Era|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天文 (元号)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天文 (元号)|1=Tenbun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1192853}} ({{ill|1542|en|1542|WD=Q6520|lt=1542|1=1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|en|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|WD=Q941979|lt=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|1=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō|en|Daidō|WD=Q1373191|lt=Daidō|1=Daidō}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|en|Uesugi clan|WD=Q1150058|lt=Uesugi clan|1=Uesugi clan}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji (Muromachi period)|en|Kōji (Muromachi period)|WD=Q1143910|lt=Kōji|1=Kōji (Muromachi period)}} ({{ill|1557|en|1557|WD=Q6595|lt=1557|1=1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|en|Uesugi Kenshin|WD=Q311080|lt=Uesugi Kenshin|1=Uesugi Kenshin}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eiroku Era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} ({{ill|1567|en|1567|WD=Q6642|lt=1567|1=1567}}) and the {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battle of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|en|Takeda clan|WD=Q1210114|lt=Takeda clan|1=Takeda clan}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|WD=Q1328185|lt=Keichō Era|1=Keichō}} (around {{ill|1600|en|1600|WD=Q6720|lt=1600|1=1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5th year 〈1600th year 〉/{{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku|1=Genroku}} 〈{{ill|1688|en|1688|WD=Q7671|lt=1688|1=1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. Table 2 shows the major historical sources related to Kosugeyama. In the descriptions that follow, the abbreviations listed in Table 2 will be used when referring to these sources. {|class="wikitable" |+'''Table 2: List of Major Historical Sources of Kosugeyama''' ! Document Name ! Abbreviation ! Date/Period ! Summary |- ! Record of the Origins of the Kosugeyama Eight Gongen and Ganryūji, Takai District, Shinano Province | Origin Record | Tenmon 11 (1542) | Describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, sacred boundaries, and its historical evolution. It is recorded under the name “別当并衆徒中.” |- ! Nagaoka Kagetora Prayer Document Draft | Kenshin Prayer Document | Kōji 3 (1557) | A prayer document issued as Ganryūji prepared for battle against Takeda Harunobu. It recounts the founding tradition and prosperity of Ganryūji and, while referencing Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, offers prayers for military success. |- ! Illustration of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Illustration of Ganryūji | Eirōku 9 (1666) | An illustration depicting the flourishing state of Kosugeyama in the medieval period, showing Ganryūji accompanied by numerous monastic quarters. The production date is questionableAs an illustration depicting the flourishing period of Kosugeyama, an illustration of Ganryūji bearing the inscription {{ill|1566|en|1566|WD=Q6638|lt=1566|1=1566}} ({{ill|Eiroku|en|Eiroku|WD=Q1143341|lt=Eiroku|1=Eiroku}}9) is known. In this illustration, it is said that there were 19 monastic quarters in the upper complex, 19 in the middle, and 11 in the lower complex, and that the main hall overseeing these—the Daisēin—had 19 subsidiary chapels. However, this illustration contradicts the timeline of the disastrous {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battle of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}} in {{ill|1561|en|1561|WD=Q6618|lt=1561|1=1561}} (Eirōku 4) as mentioned earlier. Additionally, the names of the monastic quarters and the positions of the stone walls do not correspond with the dates, raising several doubts. For these reasons, it is possible that this illustration was retrospectively drawn in the early modern period to showcase the prosperity of Kosuge, and its reliability as a historical source should be regarded with caution. [信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ編 2005:76-77]. |- ! Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Brief Origins | Composed in Keichō 5 (1600) and revised in Genroku 1 (1688) | Based on the account in the Origin Record, this document describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, and its historical evolution. It details the flourishing during the medieval period and the subsequent devastation and decline caused by the military fires of the Takeda clan, thereby forming the basis for the conventional understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} === Prehistoric Era === Similar to other Shugendō sacred sites, Mount Kosuge (小菅山) also exhibits layers of nature worship which must be acknowledged first. Around the Kosuge settlement in Iiyama city, remains of settlements dating back to the {{ill|Jōmon period|en|Jōmon period|WD=Q52824|lt=Jōmon period|1=Jōmon period}} have been discovered, and it has been confirmed that rice cultivation began by the mid-{{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|WD=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period|1=Yayoi period}}. Hence, the area around Mount Kosuge saw early settlement. Despite being one of the snowiest regions in the world adjacent to {{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}} to the north, settlement was possible due to abundant water resources from snow and forests. It is known that prior to Shugendō practices, there was worship related to this abundant natural productivity (water deity worship). === Establishment of Mount Kosuge === The historical establishment of Mount Kosuge as a religious site with shrines and temples is considered to have occurred no later than the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}. This conclusion is drawn from historical artifacts, such as the wooden seated statue of Batō Kannon, presumed to have been created in the late Heian period. The late Heian period also saw the establishment of {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=Honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} thought and the rise of the medieval Kumano pilgrimage. The area around northern Shinano, including Mount Kosuge, was influenced by Kumano Shugendō, inferred from the mention of Mount Togakushi in the {{ill|Ryōjin Hishō|en|Ryōjin Hishō|WD=Q3010584|lt=Ryōjin Hishō|1=Ryōjin Hishō}} compiled by {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|1=Emperor Go-Shirakawa}}. Numerous Kumano shrines were established alongside Hachisho Gongen, confirming Kumano Shugendō's role in establishing Kosuge's sacred area. Further evidence of Kosuge’s establishment by this time is the Bodai-in Mandala, painted in Kinai on Chinese-imported silk, dated from the late Kamakura to the {{ill|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|en|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|WD=Q8140349|lt=Nanboku-chō period|1=Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)}}. Holding such rare artifacts suggests Mount Kosuge was firmly established with significant influence. === Nanboku-chō Period to Prosperity === By the fall of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate|1=Kamakura shogunate}} and the start of the Nanboku-chō period, Kosuge was strategically located between the forces of the {{ill|Takanashi clan|en|Takanashi clan|WD=Q2975374|lt=Takanashi clan|1=Takanashi clan}} in Inukai estate to the south and the {{ill|Ichikawa clan|ja|市河氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikawa clan|1=Q11480612|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11480612}} in Shikumigō Yuyama estate to the north. In 1356, Takanashi forces of the Southern Court were defeated at Kosuge while attacking Shikumigō. The area eventually stabilized under Ashikaga shogunate rule, leading to a prosperous era as a Shugendō sacred site. Evidence of this prosperity includes the construction of Kayakiri Hall in 1422, where local lords donated paintings of the Thirty-three Manifestations of Kannon. Extensive rebuilding of Genryū-ji Temple occurred between 1430-1434, and other major constructions continued into the mid-16th century. In 1421, shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi granted Kosuge estate to Daijōin Hōin Chūi along with Wakaoji of {{ill|Zenrin-ji|en|Zenrin-ji|WD=Q189807|lt=Zenrin-ji|1=Zenrin-ji}}, establishing control from Kyoto. A similar grant occurred in 1467 by Ashikaga Yoshimasa, confirming Kosuge’s integration under Kyoto’s influence. === Sengoku Period === During the Sengoku period, Kosuge suffered from conflicts between the {{ill|Uesugi clan|en|Uesugi clan|WD=Q1150058|lt=Uesugi clan|1=Uesugi clan}} and {{ill|Takeda clan|en|Takeda clan|WD=Q1210114|lt=Takeda clan|1=Takeda clan}}. Despite temporary Takeda control, strategic importance ensured continuous habitation. By 1567, documents from Zenrin-ji note that Kosuge ceased tribute, indicating independence from Kyoto. === Early Modern Period and Later === Post-1582, Kosuge came under {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|en|Uesugi Kagekatsu|WD=Q1376605|lt=Uesugi Kagekatsu|1=Uesugi Kagekatsu}} after the fall of the Takeda. Rebuilding occurred, completed by 1591, demonstrating continued religious influence. Despite Daishōin's relocation to Aizu in 1598, local religious activities persisted, demonstrating Daishōin's lesser influence than commonly perceived. Table 3 illustrates Kosuge's consistent economic vitality, independent from Daishōin's fluctuating status. Furthermore, the secular management of rituals by villagers reinforced Kosuge’s local religious authority. === Modern Era === The Meiji government's Shinto-Buddhist separation saw the transformation of Mount Kosuge into Kosuge Shrine. Established in 1868, it became a village shrine in 1873 and a prefectural shrine in 1933. Local shrines merged in 1909, solidifying Kosuge Shrine’s modern status. == Cultural Properties within Kosuge Shrine == Kosuge Shrine contains significant cultural properties such as the main hall (Important Cultural Property) dating from mid-Muromachi, established around 1532-1554, unique for its architectural design. Other treasures include Niōmon, Satomiya, Bodai-in, and cedar avenues dating from the Edo period, along with remarkable natural and cultural landmarks detailed in Table 4. == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual is Kosuge Shrine’s principal ritual, designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|1=National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6573893}}. Traditionally held annually, it now occurs every three years in July, involving ceremonial burning of pillar pines to predict peace or harvest prosperity. == Transportation == * From JR East {{ill|Iiyama Station|en|Iiyama Station|WD=Q5995045|lt=Iiyama Station|1=Iiyama Station}} (Iiyama Line), take Nagaden bus towards Nozawa Onsen, alight at Sekizawa stop (25 min), walk 20 min. == References == {{Reflist|2}} == Further Reading == * See original text for references. == See Also == {{Commonscat|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} * {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Mount Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}} * {{ill|Shugendō|en|Shugendō|WD=Q1483875|lt=Shugendō|1=Shugendō}} * {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}} * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|WD=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano faith|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} == External Links == * [http://kosugejinja.jp/ 小菅神社] - 公式サイト * [http://www.janis.or.jp/users/ozunu/ 小菅の里] — 小菅神社が所在する小菅地区の研究・文化財保護・振興にとりくむ「小菅の里保護委員会」の公式サイト。 * [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/bunkazai/bunkazai.htm 飯山市の文化財] — [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/top.htm 飯山市ふるさと館]公式サイト内。地区の欄に瑞穂とあるのが、小菅神社神域内の文化財。種別、写真、登録日付など基礎情報。 * [http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/kosuge.html 小菅神社の里・飯山市] — 地域情報サイト「[http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/ 信州の旅.com]」内コンテンツ。 * [http://www.omiyasan.com/north/iiyama/post-56.php 小菅神社奥社] — 神社情報サイト「[http://www.omiyasan.com/ おみやさんcom]」内コンテンツ。 * 2万5千分の1 地形図「[http://watchizu.gsi.go.jp/watchizu.html?b=365346&l=1382607 往郷]」 — 国土地理院・[https://maps.gsi.go.jp/ 地図閲覧サービス]。 {{translated page|ja|小菅神社 (飯山市)|version=97011798|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Remains of Kayakiri Hall]] [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gomadō (former Daishōin site)]] [[ja:小菅神社 (飯山市)]] [[ja:小菅神社]] [[ja:歴史]] [[ja:柱松柴灯神事]] {{Commons category|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} {{wikidata link|Q11463538}} [[Category:Buildings in Iiyama]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Cultural heritage monuments in Japan]] [[Category:Cultural_heritage_monuments_in_Japan]] [[Category:En no Gyōja]] [[Category:Former Prefectural Shrines in Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:History of Iiyama]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Pages with files linked by ill]] [[Category:Shinano 33 Kannon Pilgrimage]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Shingon Buddhism]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto_shrines_in_Nagano_Prefecture]] [[Category:Shugendō]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:pages]]

Along with {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}} and {{ill|Mount Iizuna|en|Mount Iizuna|WD=Q11666652|lt=Iitsuna|1=Mount Iizuna}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Ozunu|1=En no Gyōja}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period|1=Meiji era}} due to the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|1=Shinbutsu bunri}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre-modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. == Overview ==

The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. However, according to several ancient documents that recount the shrine’s history, the Shugendō temple Ganryūji (元隆寺), founded by En no Ozunu, is considered the origin of Kosugeyama. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|en|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|WD=Q17004306|lt=Horse-Headed Kannon|1=Hayagriva (Buddhism)}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. En no Ozunu subsequently enshrined Kosuge Gongen as the principal deity and, in addition, invited and enshrined seven deities—{{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|lt=Kumano|lt_ja=熊野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=}}, {{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kanminesanjin|1=Kimpusen-ji}} ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino|1=Yoshino|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15410122}}), {{ill|Mount Haku|en|Mount Haku|WD=Q2639098|lt=Hakusan|1=Mount Haku}}, {{ill|Mount Tate|en|Mount Tate|WD=Q2977103|lt=Tateyama|1=Mount Tate}}, Sannō, Hayayuki, and {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}}—as shown in Table 1. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon Era|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天文 (元号)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天文 (元号)|1=Tenbun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1192853}} ({{ill|1542|en|1542|WD=Q6520|lt=1542|1=1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|en|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|WD=Q941979|lt=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|1=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō|en|Daidō|WD=Q1373191|lt=Daidō|1=Daidō}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|en|Uesugi clan|WD=Q1150058|lt=Uesugi clan|1=Uesugi clan}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji (Muromachi period)|en|Kōji (Muromachi period)|WD=Q1143910|lt=Kōji|1=Kōji (Muromachi period)}} ({{ill|1557|en|1557|WD=Q6595|lt=1557|1=1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|en|Uesugi Kenshin|WD=Q311080|lt=Uesugi Kenshin|1=Uesugi Kenshin}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eiroku Era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} ({{ill|1567|en|1567|WD=Q6642|lt=1567|1=1567}}) and the {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battle of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|en|Takeda clan|WD=Q1210114|lt=Takeda clan|1=Takeda clan}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|WD=Q1328185|lt=Keichō Era|1=Keichō}} (around {{ill|1600|en|1600|WD=Q6720|lt=1600|1=1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5th year 〈1600th year 〉/{{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku|1=Genroku}} 〈{{ill|1688|en|1688|WD=Q7671|lt=1688|1=1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. Table 2 shows the major historical sources related to Kosugeyama. Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Brief Origins | Composed in Keichō 5 (1600) and revised in Genroku 1 (1688) | Based on the account in the Origin Record, this document describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, and its historical evolution. It details the flourishing during the medieval period and the subsequent devastation and decline caused by the military fires of the Takeda clan, thereby forming the basis for the conventional understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} === Prehistoric Era === Similar to other Shugendō sacred sites, Mount Kosuge (小菅山) also exhibits layers of nature worship which must be acknowledged first. Around the Kosuge settlement in Iiyama city, remains of settlements dating back to the {{ill|Jōmon period|en|Jōmon period|WD=Q52824|lt=Jōmon period|1=Jōmon period}} have been discovered, and it has been confirmed that rice cultivation began by the mid-{{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|WD=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period|1=Yayoi period}}. Hence, the area around Mount Kosuge saw early settlement. Despite being one of the snowiest regions in the world adjacent to {{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}} to the north, settlement was possible due to abundant water resources from snow and forests. It is known that prior to Shugendō practices, there was worship related to this abundant natural productivity (water deity worship). === Establishment of Mount Kosuge === The historical establishment of Mount Kosuge as a religious site with shrines and temples is considered to have occurred no later than the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}. This conclusion is drawn from historical artifacts, such as the wooden seated statue of Batō Kannon, presumed to have been created in the late Heian period. The late Heian period also saw the establishment of {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=Honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} thought and the rise of the medieval Kumano pilgrimage. The area around northern Shinano, including Mount Kosuge, was influenced by Kumano Shugendō, inferred from the mention of Mount Togakushi in the {{ill|Ryōjin Hishō|en|Ryōjin Hishō|WD=Q3010584|lt=Ryōjin Hishō|1=Ryōjin Hishō}} compiled by {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|1=Emperor Go-Shirakawa}}. Numerous Kumano shrines were established alongside Hachisho Gongen, confirming Kumano Shugendō's role in establishing Kosuge's sacred area. Further evidence of Kosuge’s establishment by this time is the Bodai-in Mandala, painted in Kinai on Chinese-imported silk, dated from the late Kamakura to the {{ill|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|en|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|WD=Q8140349|lt=Nanboku-chō period|1=Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)}}. Holding such rare artifacts suggests Mount Kosuge was firmly established with significant influence. === Nanboku-chō Period to Prosperity === By the fall of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate|1=Kamakura shogunate}} and the start of the Nanboku-chō period, Kosuge was strategically located between the forces of the {{ill|Takanashi clan|en|Takanashi clan|WD=Q2975374|lt=Takanashi clan|1=Takanashi clan}} in Inukai estate to the south and the {{ill|Ichikawa clan|ja|市河氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikawa clan|1=Q11480612|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11480612}} in Shikumigō Yuyama estate to the north. In 1356, Takanashi forces of the Southern Court were defeated at Kosuge while attacking Shikumigō. The area eventually stabilized under Ashikaga shogunate rule, leading to a prosperous era as a Shugendō sacred site. Evidence of this prosperity includes the construction of Kayakiri Hall in 1422, where local lords donated paintings of the Thirty-three Manifestations of Kannon. Extensive rebuilding of Genryū-ji Temple occurred between 1430-1434, and other major constructions continued into the mid-16th century. In 1421, shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi granted Kosuge estate to Daijōin Hōin Chūi along with Wakaoji of {{ill|Zenrin-ji|en|Zenrin-ji|WD=Q189807|lt=Zenrin-ji|1=Zenrin-ji}}, establishing control from Kyoto. A similar grant occurred in 1467 by Ashikaga Yoshimasa, confirming Kosuge’s integration under Kyoto’s influence. === Sengoku Period === During the Sengoku period, Kosuge suffered from conflicts between the {{ill|Uesugi clan|en|Uesugi clan|WD=Q1150058|lt=Uesugi clan|1=Uesugi clan}} and {{ill|Takeda clan|en|Takeda clan|WD=Q1210114|lt=Takeda clan|1=Takeda clan}}. Despite temporary Takeda control, strategic importance ensured continuous habitation. By 1567, documents from Zenrin-ji note that Kosuge ceased tribute, indicating independence from Kyoto. === Early Modern Period and Later === Post-1582, Kosuge came under {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|en|Uesugi Kagekatsu|WD=Q1376605|lt=Uesugi Kagekatsu|1=Uesugi Kagekatsu}} after the fall of the Takeda. Rebuilding occurred, completed by 1591, demonstrating continued religious influence. Despite Daishōin's relocation to Aizu in 1598, local religious activities persisted, demonstrating Daishōin's lesser influence than commonly perceived. Table 3 illustrates Kosuge's consistent economic vitality, independent from Daishōin's fluctuating status. Furthermore, the secular management of rituals by villagers reinforced Kosuge’s local religious authority. === Modern Era === The Meiji government's Shinto-Buddhist separation saw the transformation of Mount Kosuge into Kosuge Shrine. Established in 1868, it became a village shrine in 1873 and a prefectural shrine in 1933. Local shrines merged in 1909, solidifying Kosuge Shrine’s modern status. == Cultural Properties within Kosuge Shrine == Kosuge Shrine contains significant cultural properties such as the main hall (Important Cultural Property) dating from mid-Muromachi, established around 1532-1554, unique for its architectural design. Other treasures include Niōmon, Satomiya, Bodai-in, and cedar avenues dating from the Edo period, along with remarkable natural and cultural landmarks detailed in Table 4. == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual is Kosuge Shrine’s principal ritual, designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|1=National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6573893}}. Traditionally held annually, it now occurs every three years in July, involving ceremonial burning of pillar pines to predict peace or harvest prosperity. == Transportation == * From JR East {{ill|Iiyama Station|en|Iiyama Station|WD=Q5995045|lt=Iiyama Station|1=Iiyama Station}} (Iiyama Line), take Nagaden bus towards Nozawa Onsen, alight at Sekizawa stop (25 min), walk 20 min. == References == {{Reflist|2}} == Further Reading == * See original text for references. == See Also == {{Commonscat|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} * {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Mount Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}} * {{ill|Shugendō|en|Shugendō|WD=Q1483875|lt=Shugendō|1=Shugendō}} * {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}} * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|WD=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano faith|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} == External Links == * [http://kosugejinja.jp/ 小菅神社] - 公式サイト * [http://www.janis.or.jp/users/ozunu/ 小菅の里] — 小菅神社が所在する小菅地区の研究・文化財保護・振興にとりくむ「小菅の里保護委員会」の公式サイト。 * [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/bunkazai/bunkazai.htm 飯山市の文化財] — [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/top.htm 飯山市ふるさと館]公式サイト内。地区の欄に瑞穂とあるのが、小菅神社神域内の文化財。種別、写真、登録日付など基礎情報。 * [http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/kosuge.html 小菅神社の里・飯山市] — 地域情報サイト「[http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/ 信州の旅.com]」内コンテンツ。 * [http://www.omiyasan.com/north/iiyama/post-56.php 小菅神社奥社] — 神社情報サイト「[http://www.omiyasan.com/ おみやさんcom]」内コンテンツ。 * 2万5千分の1 地形図「[http://watchizu.gsi.go.jp/watchizu.html?b=365346&l=1382607 往郷]」 — 国土地理院・[https://maps.gsi.go.jp/ 地図閲覧サービス]。 {{translated page|ja|小菅神社 (飯山市)|version=97011798|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Remains of Kayakiri Hall]] [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gomadō (former Daishōin site)]] [[ja:小菅神社 (飯山市)]] [[ja:小菅神社]] [[ja:歴史]] [[ja:柱松柴灯神事]] {{Commons category|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} {{wikidata link|Q11463538}} [[Category:Buildings in Iiyama]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Cultural heritage monuments in Japan]] [[Category:Cultural_heritage_monuments_in_Japan]] [[Category:En no Gyōja]] [[Category:Former Prefectural Shrines in Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:History of Iiyama]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Pages with files linked by ill]] [[Category:Shinano 33 Kannon Pilgrimage]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Shingon Buddhism]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto_shrines_in_Nagano_Prefecture]] [[Category:Shugendō]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:pages]]

Satomiya: {{coord|36|53|46.2|N|138|25|21.3|E|display=title,inline}} |religious_affiliation = {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto|1=Shinto}}|deity = Yashogongen (八所権現) |religious_affiliation = {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto|1=Shinto}}|type = Former {{ill|Village Shrine|ja|郷社|1=Gō-sha|WD=Q134917316}}{{efn|District Shrines|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Village Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}} (1872)
Former {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}} (1933) |Founding = Unknown |Main hall = Irimoya style |religious_affiliation = {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto|1=Shinto}}|festival = Sunday in mid-July |Ritual = Hashiramatsu Shibatō Ritual (every three years) |Map = {{location map+|Japan Nagano|width=210|float=center|caption=|places= {{location map~|Japan Nagano|lat_deg=36|lat_min=53|lat_sec=46.2|lon_deg=138|lon_min=25|lon_sec=21.3|position=left|label=Satomiya|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{location map~|Japan Nagano|lat_deg=36|lat_min=53|lat_sec=47.6|lon_deg=138|lon_min=26|lon_sec=7.4|position=right|label=Inner Shrine|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}}}} {{OSM location map|coord={{coord|36.895701|N|138.415382|E}}|fullscreen-option=0|zoom=11|float=center|width=200|caption=|title=|mark-coord1={{coord|36|53|46.2|N|138|25|21.3|E}}|label1=Satomiya|label-pos1=left|mark-size1=8|mark-coord2={{coord|36|53|47.6|N|138|26|7.4|E}}|label2=Inner Shrine|label-pos2=right|mark-size2=8}} |image = File:P8220544 Okusha 3.JPG |location = {{ill|Iiyama|WD=Q851097|1=Iiyama, Nagano}} |coordinates = {{Coord|36.896556|N|138.435389|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} }} '''Kosuge Shrine (小菅神社)''' is a {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|WD=Q127877|lt=Nagano Prefecture|1=Nagano Prefecture}} {{ill|Iiyama, Nagano|en|Iiyama, Nagano|WD=Q851097|lt=Iiyama|1=Iiyama, Nagano}}-based {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto Shrine|1=Shinto shrine}}. Along with {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}} and {{ill|Mount Iizuna|en|Mount Iizuna|WD=Q11666652|lt=Iitsuna|1=Mount Iizuna}}, it is one of the '''Three Great Shugendō Sacred Sites of Shinshu'''. According to various traditions, the Shugendō temple Kosugezan Ganryūji (こすげざん がんりゅうじ), founded by {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Ozunu|1=En no Gyōja}}, is the origin of Kosuge Shrine. After several periods of decline and reconstruction, it was designated as a shrine during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period|1=Meiji era}} due to the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Separation of Shinto and Buddhism|1=Shinbutsu bunri}}, and has continued to the present day. Note that in this article, the pre-modern temple (Kosugezan Ganryūji) and the modern shrine (Kosuge Shrine) are treated as a single historical entity, and the name Kosugeyama, which is also the name of the sacred site, is used as a collective term to refer to both. == Overview ==
{|class="wikitable" |+'''Table 1: Kosugeyama Eight Gongen''' ! Gongen (Divine Name) ! Source of Enshrinement ! Local Buddha |- ! {{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=}} ({{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami-no-Mikoto|1=Izanami}}) | {{ill|Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Sanzan|ja|熊野三山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Sanzan|comment=enwiki is a redirect|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} | {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|WD=Q236242|lt=Amitabha Buddha|1=Amitābha}} |- ! Konpō Gongen ([[Emperor Ankan]]) | Mount Kanmine ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino|1=Yoshino|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15410122}}) | {{ill|Shakyamuni Tathāgata Buddha|ja|釈迦如来|1=Shakyamuni Tathāgata|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakyamuni Tathāgata Buddha|qq=}} |- ! {{ill|Hakusan Gongen|ja|白山権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakusan Gongen|qq=}} ({{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi-no-Mikoto|1=Izanagi}}) | Hakusan | {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|Ekādaśamukha|WD=Q11404731|lt=Eleven-Faced Kannon|1=Ekādaśamukha}} |- ! {{ill|Tateyama Gongen|ja|立山権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tateyama Gongen|qq=}} ({{ill|Kunitama|en|Kunitama|WD=Q9692242|WD=Q276944|lt=Okuninushi-no-Mikoto|1=Kunitama}}) | Tateyama | {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|WD=Q236242|lt=Amitabha Buddha|1=Amitābha}} |- ! {{ill|Sannō Gongen|ja|山王権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sannō Gongen|comment=enwiki is a redirect|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} ({{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944|WD=Q276944|lt=Okuninushi-no-Mikoto|1=Ōkuninushi}}) | Zao | {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Yakushi Nyorai Medicine Buddha|1=Bhaisajyaguru}} |- ! Togakushi Gongen ({{ill|Ame-no-Tajikarao|en|Ame-no-Tajikarao|WD=Q849412|lt=The Strong-Handed Deity|1=Ame-no-Tajikarao}}) | Togakushi Mountain | {{ill|Āryāvalokiteśvara|ja|聖観音|1=Āryāvalokiteśvara|lt=Shō Kannon|lt_ja=正観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Āryāvalokiteśvara|13=User:Immanuelle/Āryāvalokiteśvara|qq=}} |- ! Kosuge Gongen ({{ill|Matarajin|en|Matarajin|WD=Q6380689|lt=Matarajin|1=Matarajin}}) | (Kosugeyama Main Deity) | {{ill|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|en|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|WD=Q17004306|lt=Horse-Headed Kannon|1=Hayagriva (Buddhism)}} |}
The exact founding date of Kosugeyama remains unclear. However, according to several ancient documents that recount the shrine’s history, the Shugendō temple Ganryūji (元隆寺), founded by En no Ozunu, is considered the origin of Kosugeyama. To summarize these records: while En no Ozunu was journeying through various provinces in search of a land worthy of propagating Buddhist teachings, he encountered Kosugeyama. Deeply moved by a landscape filled with sacred trees and spiritual herbs, he was visited by the local land deity. This deity proclaimed that the land was a gathering place of many gods, ideally suited for the spread of Buddhism, and that it would bestow its own protection. Upon receiving this divine message, as En no Ozunu devoted himself to prayer, Kosuge Gongen appeared. Declaring himself an incarnation of {{ill|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|en|Hayagriva (Buddhism)|WD=Q17004306|lt=Horse-Headed Kannon|1=Hayagriva (Buddhism)}}, he vowed to support the protection and flourishing of Buddhist doctrine. En no Ozunu subsequently enshrined Kosuge Gongen as the principal deity and, in addition, invited and enshrined seven deities—{{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|lt=Kumano|lt_ja=熊野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Gongen|qq=}}, {{ill|Kimpusen-ji|en|Kimpusen-ji|WD=Q1741668|lt=Kanminesanjin|1=Kimpusen-ji}} ({{ill|Yoshino|ja|吉野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshino|1=Yoshino|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15410122}}), {{ill|Mount Haku|en|Mount Haku|WD=Q2639098|lt=Hakusan|1=Mount Haku}}, {{ill|Mount Tate|en|Mount Tate|WD=Q2977103|lt=Tateyama|1=Mount Tate}}, Sannō, Hayayuki, and {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}}—as shown in Table 1. The oldest document conveying this tradition is likely the “Record of the Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (信州高井郡小菅山八所権現元隆寺来由記), authored under the name of the chief monk of the congregation, dated to the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmon Era|ja|天文 (日本)|lt=Tenmon|lt_ja=天文|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmon Era|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天文 (元号)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天文 (元号)|1=Tenbun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1192853}} ({{ill|1542|en|1542|WD=Q6520|lt=1542|1=1542}}). Furthermore, the document relates that, in acknowledgment of the pacification of the eastern barbarians’ rebellion by the divine might of the Eight Gongen, {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|en|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|WD=Q941979|lt=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|1=Sakanoue no Tamuramaro}} visited this region during the {{ill|Daidō|en|Daidō|WD=Q1373191|lt=Daidō|1=Daidō}} period. There, he not only rebuilt the principal shrine of the Eight Gongen and the Kayayorikidō but also established Ganryūji and organized various pagodas and halls. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|WD=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, the entire Kosugeyama area was placed under the protection of the {{ill|Uesugi clan|en|Uesugi clan|WD=Q1150058|lt=Uesugi clan|1=Uesugi clan}}. Notably, a prayer document from the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kōji (Muromachi period)|en|Kōji (Muromachi period)|WD=Q1143910|lt=Kōji|1=Kōji (Muromachi period)}} ({{ill|1557|en|1557|WD=Q6595|lt=1557|1=1557}}) of {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|en|Uesugi Kenshin|WD=Q311080|lt=Uesugi Kenshin|1=Uesugi Kenshin}} has attracted attention for its reference to the tradition of Kosugeyama. In this document, Kenshin, invoking the name of Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, prayed for military success, reflecting the widespread devotion to Kosugeyama. However, this period of prosperity lasted only until the 10th year of the {{ill|Eiroku Era|ja|Eiroku|lt=Eiroku|lt_ja=Eiroku|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eiroku Era|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} ({{ill|1567|en|1567|WD=Q6642|lt=1567|1=1567}}) and the {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battle of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}}, when Ganryūji, save for its main hall, was completely burned down by the forces of the {{ill|Takeda clan|en|Takeda clan|WD=Q1210114|lt=Takeda clan|1=Takeda clan}} pursuing the defeated Uesugi army. Subsequently, due to repeated warfare, Ganryūji was left unoccupied, and by the first year of the {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|WD=Q1328185|lt=Keichō Era|1=Keichō}} (around {{ill|1600|en|1600|WD=Q6720|lt=1600|1=1600}}) it had fallen entirely into ruins. According to the “Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province” (慶長5th year 〈1600th year 〉/{{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku|1=Genroku}} 〈{{ill|1688|en|1688|WD=Q7671|lt=1688|1=1688}}〉), even after nearly a century had passed, no reconstruction was undertaken, and the former temple complex had reverted to fields, houses, and barren land. == History == The understanding of Kosugeyama’s tradition – that it was founded by En no Ozunu, flourished, and later declined due to the military devastation inflicted by the Takeda clan – was established from the Sengoku period to the early modern period. This interpretation is not only widely believed locally but has also frequently been regarded as the conventional view in historiography, supported by several influential ancient documents. However, when one considers the nature of the various historical sources that describe the process from prosperity to decline, it is difficult to accept their accounts as straightforward historical facts. One of the principal sources conveying this tradition is the Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province. This document was written in Keichō 5 (1600) and is said to have been revised in Genroku 1 (1688). Moreover, the document was not only produced by the head abbot of Ganryūji but was also printed on woodblocks and distributed—a project that would have required a significant amount of funding. If Ganryūji had truly been left to decline after suffering the military fires of the Takeda clan, it would be unnatural to suppose that such an undertaking could have been realized.信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ[2005: 73-74]。 Recent research on Kosugeyama—integrating local folklore studies and other historical sources—is revealing a history that differs somewhat from the traditional account described above. Table 2 shows the major historical sources related to Kosugeyama. In the descriptions that follow, the abbreviations listed in Table 2 will be used when referring to these sources. {|class="wikitable" |+'''Table 2: List of Major Historical Sources of Kosugeyama''' ! Document Name ! Abbreviation ! Date/Period ! Summary |- ! Record of the Origins of the Kosugeyama Eight Gongen and Ganryūji, Takai District, Shinano Province | Origin Record | Tenmon 11 (1542) | Describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, sacred boundaries, and its historical evolution. It is recorded under the name “別当并衆徒中.” |- ! Nagaoka Kagetora Prayer Document Draft | Kenshin Prayer Document | Kōji 3 (1557) | A prayer document issued as Ganryūji prepared for battle against Takeda Harunobu. It recounts the founding tradition and prosperity of Ganryūji and, while referencing Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, offers prayers for military success. |- ! Illustration of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Illustration of Ganryūji | Eirōku 9 (1666) | An illustration depicting the flourishing state of Kosugeyama in the medieval period, showing Ganryūji accompanied by numerous monastic quarters. The production date is questionableAs an illustration depicting the flourishing period of Kosugeyama, an illustration of Ganryūji bearing the inscription {{ill|1566|en|1566|WD=Q6638|lt=1566|1=1566}} ({{ill|Eiroku|en|Eiroku|WD=Q1143341|lt=Eiroku|1=Eiroku}}9) is known. In this illustration, it is said that there were 19 monastic quarters in the upper complex, 19 in the middle, and 11 in the lower complex, and that the main hall overseeing these—the Daisēin—had 19 subsidiary chapels. However, this illustration contradicts the timeline of the disastrous {{ill|Battles of Kawanakajima|en|Battles of Kawanakajima|WD=Q1143044|lt=Battle of Kawanakajima|1=Battles of Kawanakajima}} in {{ill|1561|en|1561|WD=Q6618|lt=1561|1=1561}} (Eirōku 4) as mentioned earlier. Additionally, the names of the monastic quarters and the positions of the stone walls do not correspond with the dates, raising several doubts. For these reasons, it is possible that this illustration was retrospectively drawn in the early modern period to showcase the prosperity of Kosuge, and its reliability as a historical source should be regarded with caution. [信州大学・飯山市小菅研究グループ編 2005:76-77]. |- ! Brief Origins of Ganryūji of Kosugeyama, Takai District, Shinano Province | Brief Origins | Composed in Keichō 5 (1600) and revised in Genroku 1 (1688) | Based on the account in the Origin Record, this document describes the founding tradition of Ganryūji, its enshrined deities, the monastic quarters, and its historical evolution. It details the flourishing during the medieval period and the subsequent devastation and decline caused by the military fires of the Takeda clan, thereby forming the basis for the conventional understanding of Kosugeyama’s historical development. |} === Prehistoric Era === Similar to other Shugendō sacred sites, Mount Kosuge (小菅山) also exhibits layers of nature worship which must be acknowledged first. Around the Kosuge settlement in Iiyama city, remains of settlements dating back to the {{ill|Jōmon period|en|Jōmon period|WD=Q52824|lt=Jōmon period|1=Jōmon period}} have been discovered, and it has been confirmed that rice cultivation began by the mid-{{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|WD=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period|1=Yayoi period}}. Hence, the area around Mount Kosuge saw early settlement. Despite being one of the snowiest regions in the world adjacent to {{ill|Echigo Province|en|Echigo Province|WD=Q666514|lt=Echigo Province|1=Echigo Province}} to the north, settlement was possible due to abundant water resources from snow and forests. It is known that prior to Shugendō practices, there was worship related to this abundant natural productivity (water deity worship). === Establishment of Mount Kosuge === The historical establishment of Mount Kosuge as a religious site with shrines and temples is considered to have occurred no later than the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}. This conclusion is drawn from historical artifacts, such as the wooden seated statue of Batō Kannon, presumed to have been created in the late Heian period. The late Heian period also saw the establishment of {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=Honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} thought and the rise of the medieval Kumano pilgrimage. The area around northern Shinano, including Mount Kosuge, was influenced by Kumano Shugendō, inferred from the mention of Mount Togakushi in the {{ill|Ryōjin Hishō|en|Ryōjin Hishō|WD=Q3010584|lt=Ryōjin Hishō|1=Ryōjin Hishō}} compiled by {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|1=Emperor Go-Shirakawa}}. Numerous Kumano shrines were established alongside Hachisho Gongen, confirming Kumano Shugendō's role in establishing Kosuge's sacred area. Further evidence of Kosuge’s establishment by this time is the Bodai-in Mandala, painted in Kinai on Chinese-imported silk, dated from the late Kamakura to the {{ill|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|en|Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)|WD=Q8140349|lt=Nanboku-chō period|1=Northern and Southern Courts period (disambiguation)}}. Holding such rare artifacts suggests Mount Kosuge was firmly established with significant influence. === Nanboku-chō Period to Prosperity === By the fall of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate|1=Kamakura shogunate}} and the start of the Nanboku-chō period, Kosuge was strategically located between the forces of the {{ill|Takanashi clan|en|Takanashi clan|WD=Q2975374|lt=Takanashi clan|1=Takanashi clan}} in Inukai estate to the south and the {{ill|Ichikawa clan|ja|市河氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikawa clan|1=Q11480612|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11480612}} in Shikumigō Yuyama estate to the north. In 1356, Takanashi forces of the Southern Court were defeated at Kosuge while attacking Shikumigō. The area eventually stabilized under Ashikaga shogunate rule, leading to a prosperous era as a Shugendō sacred site. Evidence of this prosperity includes the construction of Kayakiri Hall in 1422, where local lords donated paintings of the Thirty-three Manifestations of Kannon. Extensive rebuilding of Genryū-ji Temple occurred between 1430-1434, and other major constructions continued into the mid-16th century. In 1421, shogun Ashikaga Yoshimochi granted Kosuge estate to Daijōin Hōin Chūi along with Wakaoji of {{ill|Zenrin-ji|en|Zenrin-ji|WD=Q189807|lt=Zenrin-ji|1=Zenrin-ji}}, establishing control from Kyoto. A similar grant occurred in 1467 by Ashikaga Yoshimasa, confirming Kosuge’s integration under Kyoto’s influence. === Sengoku Period === During the Sengoku period, Kosuge suffered from conflicts between the {{ill|Uesugi clan|en|Uesugi clan|WD=Q1150058|lt=Uesugi clan|1=Uesugi clan}} and {{ill|Takeda clan|en|Takeda clan|WD=Q1210114|lt=Takeda clan|1=Takeda clan}}. Despite temporary Takeda control, strategic importance ensured continuous habitation. By 1567, documents from Zenrin-ji note that Kosuge ceased tribute, indicating independence from Kyoto. === Early Modern Period and Later === Post-1582, Kosuge came under {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|en|Uesugi Kagekatsu|WD=Q1376605|lt=Uesugi Kagekatsu|1=Uesugi Kagekatsu}} after the fall of the Takeda. Rebuilding occurred, completed by 1591, demonstrating continued religious influence. Despite Daishōin's relocation to Aizu in 1598, local religious activities persisted, demonstrating Daishōin's lesser influence than commonly perceived. Table 3 illustrates Kosuge's consistent economic vitality, independent from Daishōin's fluctuating status. Furthermore, the secular management of rituals by villagers reinforced Kosuge’s local religious authority. === Modern Era === The Meiji government's Shinto-Buddhist separation saw the transformation of Mount Kosuge into Kosuge Shrine. Established in 1868, it became a village shrine in 1873 and a prefectural shrine in 1933. Local shrines merged in 1909, solidifying Kosuge Shrine’s modern status. == Cultural Properties within Kosuge Shrine == Kosuge Shrine contains significant cultural properties such as the main hall (Important Cultural Property) dating from mid-Muromachi, established around 1532-1554, unique for its architectural design. Other treasures include Niōmon, Satomiya, Bodai-in, and cedar avenues dating from the Edo period, along with remarkable natural and cultural landmarks detailed in Table 4. == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual (柱松柴灯神事) == Hashiramatsu Shibato Ritual is Kosuge Shrine’s principal ritual, designated as a National {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|1=National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6573893}}. Traditionally held annually, it now occurs every three years in July, involving ceremonial burning of pillar pines to predict peace or harvest prosperity. == Transportation == * From JR East {{ill|Iiyama Station|en|Iiyama Station|WD=Q5995045|lt=Iiyama Station|1=Iiyama Station}} (Iiyama Line), take Nagaden bus towards Nozawa Onsen, alight at Sekizawa stop (25 min), walk 20 min. == References == {{Reflist|2}} == Further Reading == * See original text for references. == See Also == {{Commonscat|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} * {{ill|Mount Togakushi|en|Mount Togakushi|WD=Q11496659|lt=Mount Togakushi|1=Mount Togakushi}} * {{ill|Shugendō|en|Shugendō|WD=Q1483875|lt=Shugendō|1=Shugendō}} * {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}} * {{ill|Kumano faith|ja|熊野信仰|1=Kumano Faith|2=ja|3=熊野信仰|WD=Q135501741}}{{efn|The religion of [[Kumano Shrines]]|1=Kumano shrine|lt=Kumano Three Shrines|lt=Kumano faith|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano faith|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 熊野三山}} == External Links == * [http://kosugejinja.jp/ 小菅神社] - 公式サイト * [http://www.janis.or.jp/users/ozunu/ 小菅の里] — 小菅神社が所在する小菅地区の研究・文化財保護・振興にとりくむ「小菅の里保護委員会」の公式サイト。 * [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/bunkazai/bunkazai.htm 飯山市の文化財] — [http://www.city.iiyama.nagano.jp/gyousei-jouhou/gj-kanrigakusyu/furusato/top.htm 飯山市ふるさと館]公式サイト内。地区の欄に瑞穂とあるのが、小菅神社神域内の文化財。種別、写真、登録日付など基礎情報。 * [http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/kosuge.html 小菅神社の里・飯山市] — 地域情報サイト「[http://www.shinshu-tabi.com/ 信州の旅.com]」内コンテンツ。 * [http://www.omiyasan.com/north/iiyama/post-56.php 小菅神社奥社] — 神社情報サイト「[http://www.omiyasan.com/ おみやさんcom]」内コンテンツ。 * 2万5千分の1 地形図「[http://watchizu.gsi.go.jp/watchizu.html?b=365346&l=1382607 往郷]」 — 国土地理院・[https://maps.gsi.go.jp/ 地図閲覧サービス]。 {{translated page|ja|小菅神社 (飯山市)|version=97011798|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[image:P8220527_Kayakiri_temple_remains.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Remains of Kayakiri Hall]] [[image:P8220516_Gomado.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gomadō (former Daishōin site)]] [[ja:小菅神社 (飯山市)]] [[ja:小菅神社]] [[ja:歴史]] [[ja:柱松柴灯神事]] {{Commons category|Kosuge shrine, Iiyama}} {{wikidata link|Q11463538}} [[Category:Buildings in Iiyama]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:Cultural heritage monuments in Japan]] [[Category:Cultural_heritage_monuments_in_Japan]] [[Category:En no Gyōja]] [[Category:Former Prefectural Shrines in Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:History of Iiyama]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Pages with files linked by ill]] [[Category:Shinano 33 Kannon Pilgrimage]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Shingon Buddhism]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Nagano Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto_shrines_in_Nagano_Prefecture]] [[Category:Shugendō]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:pages]]
